extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

“What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.

In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain.
Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.
That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program.
Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.
Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.

In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.

Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers.
However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection.
These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.
Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers.
As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country.
Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year.

In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.
Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta.

But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs.

In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements.

He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain.
The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.
Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants.

The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year.
Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants.
But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants.
In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says.

Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law.

The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid.
“No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating.
The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world.

Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.” These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores. New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

extraction.body: The AI boom is spawning a wave of data center construction demand in the UK, but insufficient grid connection capacity is forcing some developers to change their energy plans. National Gas, the operator of the UK's gas transmission network, disclosed that large data center projects inquiring with the company about gas connection options have risen to 24 from 5 last year. The direct driver of this shift is excessively long grid connection queues. A combination of factors—planning approvals, regulatory procedures, construction costs and skilled-labor shortages—means some projects must wait years from application to actual connection to the UK's national electricity system. Under these circumstances, some developers are beginning to consider building their own gas-fired generation facilities to meet power needs during the initial phase of project operation. The Quest Park data center campus in Bedfordshire is a typical case. The project has a planned power demand of 720 megawatts and is expected to become one of the UK's largest data center campuses, but constrained by local grid capacity, it is not expected to formally connect to the power system until 2034 at the earliest. A high-pressure gas pipeline happens to pass near the campus, and connection could come significantly earlier, so the developer plans to build a gas-fired power plant first to supply power at least for the project's relatively smaller initial phase. Such considerations are not isolated. The £3 billion (approximately $4.0 billion) SDC M40 Campus in Buckinghamshire, as well as a proposed data center project by Curtis Hall in Cardiff, are both evaluating gas-fired generation as a transitional solution until formal grid connection permits are obtained, according to planning documents. Alan Fotheringham, director of low-carbon global market solutions at consultancy Jacobs, noted that the path to gas-fired generation is much shorter than the path to securing permanent grid connection capacity. The potential incremental demand for gas should not be underestimated. Marten Ford, an analyst at energy research firm Aurora Energy Research, estimates that if data center construction accelerates and renewable energy growth fails to outpace existing plans, UK gas-fired generation could increase by 40 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 44% of the country's gas-fired generation last year. He also emphasized that without broader countermeasures, large-scale deployment of data centers will drive up natural gas use and thereby increase carbon emissions. The above estimates already assume that most proposed projects are speculative investments that will ultimately not materialize. If all these projects were built, the increase in gas demand would be even more significant. Tom Edwards, an analyst at market analysis firm Cornwall Insight, also noted that regardless of the scale of construction, existing gas-fired power plants will need to run more frequently; even if data centers successfully connect to the national grid, the electricity they use comes from a mix of renewables, nuclear and natural gas, which would likewise drive gas demand to some extent. Faced with enormous demand, the UK government has begun adjusting policy. A proposal introduced last week suggests that data centers of strategic importance may be paired with gas-fired generation, provided investors commit that the long-term goal remains connection to the national grid. The proposal is accompanied by a new "commitment agreement" mechanism for data centers, under which paired power plants would not need to undergo separate carbon emissions assessments, with the relevant emissions impact handled by the government at the national level. Within the UK energy industry, there is disagreement over what energy source data centers should use. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy, the UK's largest oil, gas and electricity retailer, disagrees with the view that only natural gas and nuclear power can meet data centers' need for stable electricity supply. He proposes locating more data centers in Scotland to take advantage of the region's abundant wind resources. But real-world constraints are also evident. Many operators want to be close to customer-concentrated areas such as London, while the UK's current electricity market mechanisms lack sufficient incentives for developers to relocate projects to regions richer in renewable energy resources. Wind and solar power face land-use requirements and intermittency issues, energy storage systems are relatively costly, and small modular nuclear reactors remain some distance from large-scale commercial deployment. By contrast, the UK's existing gas pipeline network has broad coverage, and some projects can obtain gas supply more quickly. Real estate consultancy Savills said the market is currently studying multiple energy configuration options, but for some projects that need stable power supply quickly in the near term, natural gas still holds practical appeal. On the environmental front, Natascha Hospedales, head of AI affairs at ClientEarth, criticized the UK government's proposal as amounting to "tacitly allowing data centers to begin construction without simultaneously imposing equally strict environmental constraints." Katie Berriman-Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at tech industry group Tech UK, said that for most developers, the current priority remains advancing reform of the grid connection mechanism and improving related policies so projects can connect faster. In her view, gas-fired generation is more of a realistic transitional measure against the backdrop of long-term grid capacity constraints, rather than a direction of proactive industry transformation. A key variable is the actual scale of projects that materialize. Consultancies estimate that of the data center projects currently queued for grid connection, totaling 73 gigawatts of installed capacity, only 10% to 20% will ultimately be built. passages: The AI boom is spawning a wave of data center construction demand in the UK, but insufficient grid connection capacity is forcing some developers to change their energy plans. National Gas, the operator of the UK's gas transmission network, disclosed that large data center projects inquiring with the company about gas connection options have risen to 24 from 5 last year.

The direct driver of this shift is excessively long grid connection queues. A combination of factors—planning approvals, regulatory procedures, construction costs and skilled-labor shortages—means some projects must wait years from application to actual connection to the UK's national electricity system. Under these circumstances, some developers are beginning to consider building their own gas-fired generation facilities to meet power needs during the initial phase of project operation.

The Quest Park data center campus in Bedfordshire is a typical case. The project has a planned power demand of 720 megawatts and is expected to become one of the UK's largest data center campuses, but constrained by local grid capacity, it is not expected to formally connect to the power system until 2034 at the earliest. A high-pressure gas pipeline happens to pass near the campus, and connection could come significantly earlier, so the developer plans to build a gas-fired power plant first to supply power at least for the project's relatively smaller initial phase.

Such considerations are not isolated. The £3 billion (approximately $4.0 billion) SDC M40 Campus in Buckinghamshire, as well as a proposed data center project by Curtis Hall in Cardiff, are both evaluating gas-fired generation as a transitional solution until formal grid connection permits are obtained, according to planning documents. Alan Fotheringham, director of low-carbon global market solutions at consultancy Jacobs, noted that the path to gas-fired generation is much shorter than the path to securing permanent grid connection capacity.

The potential incremental demand for gas should not be underestimated. Marten Ford, an analyst at energy research firm Aurora Energy Research, estimates that if data center construction accelerates and renewable energy growth fails to outpace existing plans, UK gas-fired generation could increase by 40 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 44% of the country's gas-fired generation last year. He also emphasized that without broader countermeasures, large-scale deployment of data centers will drive up natural gas use and thereby increase carbon emissions.

The above estimates already assume that most proposed projects are speculative investments that will ultimately not materialize. If all these projects were built, the increase in gas demand would be even more significant. Tom Edwards, an analyst at market analysis firm Cornwall Insight, also noted that regardless of the scale of construction, existing gas-fired power plants will need to run more frequently; even if data centers successfully connect to the national grid, the electricity they use comes from a mix of renewables, nuclear and natural gas, which would likewise drive gas demand to some extent.

Faced with enormous demand, the UK government has begun adjusting policy. A proposal introduced last week suggests that data centers of strategic importance may be paired with gas-fired generation, provided investors commit that the long-term goal remains connection to the national grid. The proposal is accompanied by a new "commitment agreement" mechanism for data centers, under which paired power plants would not need to undergo separate carbon emissions assessments, with the relevant emissions impact handled by the government at the national level.

Within the UK energy industry, there is disagreement over what energy source data centers should use. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy, the UK's largest oil, gas and electricity retailer, disagrees with the view that only natural gas and nuclear power can meet data centers' need for stable electricity supply. He proposes locating more data centers in Scotland to take advantage of the region's abundant wind resources.

But real-world constraints are also evident. Many operators want to be close to customer-concentrated areas such as London, while the UK's current electricity market mechanisms lack sufficient incentives for developers to relocate projects to regions richer in renewable energy resources. Wind and solar power face land-use requirements and intermittency issues, energy storage systems are relatively costly, and small modular nuclear reactors remain some distance from large-scale commercial deployment. By contrast, the UK's existing gas pipeline network has broad coverage, and some projects can obtain gas supply more quickly. Real estate consultancy Savills said the market is currently studying multiple energy configuration options, but for some projects that need stable power supply quickly in the near term, natural gas still holds practical appeal.

On the environmental front, Natascha Hospedales, head of AI affairs at ClientEarth, criticized the UK government's proposal as amounting to "tacitly allowing data centers to begin construction without simultaneously imposing equally strict environmental constraints."

Katie Berriman-Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at tech industry group Tech UK, said that for most developers, the current priority remains advancing reform of the grid connection mechanism and improving related policies so projects can connect faster. The practices of other European countries offer a reference. Ford mentioned that Ireland has introduced regulations requiring 80% of data centers' electricity to come from renewable sources, which could serve as a reference model for promoting greater use of clean energy in data centers.

extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.” These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores. New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

extraction.body: The AI boom is spawning a wave of data center construction demand in the UK, but insufficient grid connection capacity is forcing some developers to change their energy plans. National Gas, the operator of the UK's gas transmission network, disclosed that large data center projects inquiring with the company about gas connection options have risen to 24 from 5 last year. The direct driver of this shift is excessively long grid connection queues. A combination of factors—planning approvals, regulatory procedures, construction costs and skilled-labor shortages—means some projects must wait years from application to actual connection to the UK's national electricity system. Under these circumstances, some developers are beginning to consider building their own gas-fired generation facilities to meet power needs during the initial phase of project operation. The Quest Park data center campus in Bedfordshire is a typical case. The project has a planned power demand of 720 megawatts and is expected to become one of the UK's largest data center campuses, but constrained by local grid capacity, it is not expected to formally connect to the power system until 2034 at the earliest. A high-pressure gas pipeline happens to pass near the campus, and connection could come significantly earlier, so the developer plans to build a gas-fired power plant first to supply power at least for the project's relatively smaller initial phase. Such considerations are not isolated. The £3 billion (approximately $4.0 billion) SDC M40 Campus in Buckinghamshire, as well as a proposed data center project by Curtis Hall in Cardiff, are both evaluating gas-fired generation as a transitional solution until formal grid connection permits are obtained, according to planning documents. Alan Fotheringham, director of low-carbon global market solutions at consultancy Jacobs, noted that the path to gas-fired generation is much shorter than the path to securing permanent grid connection capacity. The potential incremental demand for gas should not be underestimated. Marten Ford, an analyst at energy research firm Aurora Energy Research, estimates that if data center construction accelerates and renewable energy growth fails to outpace existing plans, UK gas-fired generation could increase by 40 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 44% of the country's gas-fired generation last year. He also emphasized that without broader countermeasures, large-scale deployment of data centers will drive up natural gas use and thereby increase carbon emissions. The above estimates already assume that most proposed projects are speculative investments that will ultimately not materialize. If all these projects were built, the increase in gas demand would be even more significant. Tom Edwards, an analyst at market analysis firm Cornwall Insight, also noted that regardless of the scale of construction, existing gas-fired power plants will need to run more frequently; even if data centers successfully connect to the national grid, the electricity they use comes from a mix of renewables, nuclear and natural gas, which would likewise drive gas demand to some extent. Faced with enormous demand, the UK government has begun adjusting policy. A proposal introduced last week suggests that data centers of strategic importance may be paired with gas-fired generation, provided investors commit that the long-term goal remains connection to the national grid. The proposal is accompanied by a new "commitment agreement" mechanism for data centers, under which paired power plants would not need to undergo separate carbon emissions assessments, with the relevant emissions impact handled by the government at the national level. Within the UK energy industry, there is disagreement over what energy source data centers should use. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy, the UK's largest oil, gas and electricity retailer, disagrees with the view that only natural gas and nuclear power can meet data centers' need for stable electricity supply. He proposes locating more data centers in Scotland to take advantage of the region's abundant wind resources. But real-world constraints are also evident. Many operators want to be close to customer-concentrated areas such as London, while the UK's current electricity market mechanisms lack sufficient incentives for developers to relocate projects to regions richer in renewable energy resources. Wind and solar power face land-use requirements and intermittency issues, energy storage systems are relatively costly, and small modular nuclear reactors remain some distance from large-scale commercial deployment. By contrast, the UK's existing gas pipeline network has broad coverage, and some projects can obtain gas supply more quickly. Real estate consultancy Savills said the market is currently studying multiple energy configuration options, but for some projects that need stable power supply quickly in the near term, natural gas still holds practical appeal. On the environmental front, Natascha Hospedales, head of AI affairs at ClientEarth, criticized the UK government's proposal as amounting to "tacitly allowing data centers to begin construction without simultaneously imposing equally strict environmental constraints." Katie Berriman-Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at tech industry group Tech UK, said that for most developers, the current priority remains advancing reform of the grid connection mechanism and improving related policies so projects can connect faster. In her view, gas-fired generation is more of a realistic transitional measure against the backdrop of long-term grid capacity constraints, rather than a direction of proactive industry transformation. A key variable is the actual scale of projects that materialize. Consultancies estimate that of the data center projects currently queued for grid connection, totaling 73 gigawatts of installed capacity, only 10% to 20% will ultimately be built. UK authorities are trying to accelerate reform of the connection queue while weeding out speculative projects that have no substantive plans to materialize. The practices of other European countries offer a reference. Ford mentioned that Ireland has introduced regulations requiring 80% of data centers' electricity to come from renewable sources, which could serve as a reference model for promoting greater use of clean energy in data centers. For the market, this trend means UK gas demand could gain a new source of growth beyond the power system, and utilization of gas-fired generation and pipeline assets may rise accordingly; but at the same time, the pace at which data center projects materialize, the progress of grid connection reform and the specific implementation standards of the government's "commitment agreements" will all directly affect the actual scale of incremental gas demand. For data center developers, whether they can strike a balance between power supply and emissions-reduction commitments is becoming a key variable in whether projects can be commissioned on schedule. passages: 1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems.
The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident.

An attacker who got into a 1Password employee’s corporate GitHub account went on to copy account records for some of the company’s users and source code from private repositories, the password manager maker disclosed on Wednesday.

“On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” the company detailed.
The post doesn’t explain how the employee’s access was obtained, and it gives no date for when the intruder was detected or shut out.
“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated.

The keys that protect vaults and the account recovery keys weren’t reached either, with the company reporting that its apps, browser extensions and services kept working normally. “1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys,” it added.

The records pulled down by the malicious code belong to “a subset of our users,” and 1Password hasn’t said how many people that covers or whether individual, business or family accounts were affected. The rest was internal metadata, “version numeric identifiers” and “file numeric identifiers” tied to its internal architecture, which the company lists as non-secret.
The attacker also got into the company’s CI/CD system. “Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets,” 1Password noted. Infrastructure secrets kept in CI/CD have been rotated.

“On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” the company detailed.
The post doesn’t explain how the employee’s access was obtained, and it gives no date for when the intruder was detected or shut out.
“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated.

The keys that protect vaults and the account recovery keys weren’t reached either, with the company reporting that its apps, browser extensions and services kept working normally. “1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys,” it added.

The records pulled down by the malicious code belong to “a subset of our users,” and 1Password hasn’t said how many people that covers or whether individual, business or family accounts were affected. Each record holds the name and email address a customer uses with 1Password, account and user identifiers, the date the account was created and the time of its last sign-in.

The attacker also got the public keys tied to those accounts, which are “public by design” and have “no impact to user security,” the company noted. Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters were taken too, and 1Password maintains these “cannot be used to access your account.”

Another part of the haul affects a smaller group. Tokens from invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails were copied, though a token only works “when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code.”

1Password has since lengthened the code from six digits to ten alphanumeric characters and contacted the small number of users affected. So far, the company has “validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.”
The rest was internal metadata, “version numeric identifiers” and “file numeric identifiers” tied to its internal architecture, which the company lists as non-secret.
The attacker also got into the company’s CI/CD system. “Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets,” 1Password noted. Infrastructure secrets kept in CI/CD have been rotated.
The compromised GitHub account was disabled, the token the attacker stole revoked and the access the attacker had set up removed. Internal credentials that may have leaked were rotated or revoked.
On top of that, 1Password said it has tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, added new detections, and brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate the cleanup.

No action is needed on customers’ accounts, 1Password advised. “We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password,” the post reads , and the warning extends to texts and phone calls that mention invitations or account recovery.

There are plenty of great options to choose from, which will likely suit the needs of different users. Whether you’re looking to put a massive virtual screen in front of your eyes, record videos without reaching for your phone, or experiment with wearable AI, you have something for everyone. And the savings aren’t bad, either. XREAL is knocking $100 off its One Pro glasses, VITURE has discounted its Luma Ultra by $150, and Meta is offering 25% off selected Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses. So I’ve narrowed things down to six deals worth checking out, covering everything from gaming and portable entertainment to hands-free photography and AI assistance. XREAL has a great deal for you if you’re looking to turn any compatible device into a massive personal screen. The XREAL One Pro is a great deal, which basically turns it into a wearable display that lets you enjoy movies, games, and even desktop applications without needing a physical monitor in front of you. At $499, down from $599, the One Pro is worth considering if you’ve been waiting to try a high-end wearable display. INAIR Pod is an ideal companion for compatible AR glasses, bringing Android apps and spatial computing to selected models from VITURE, XREAL, and RayNeo. Run supported apps directly on the Pod and create a workspace with up to six virtual windows in supported INAIR configurations. Spatial features and window availability vary by glasses model. Get it for $351.99, down from $439.99 . For an integrated setup, the INAIR 2 Go Pack puts a portable spatial workstation in your bag. It combines INAIR 2 Pro glasses, INAIR Pod, a foldable keyboard, and a carrying case for work and entertainment on the go—from browsing and writing to watching your favorite content. Get the bundle for $799.20, down from $999 . Ray-Ban Meta glasses are still one of the easiest ways to try smart eyewear without committing to something that looks a little too futuristic. The second-generation models retain Ray-Ban’s familiar styling while adding an upgraded camera, improved battery life, and Meta AI integration. You get a 12MP camera capable of recording video at up to 3K resolution, along with open-ear speakers and microphones for music, phone calls, and voice commands. Meta AI can also help answer questions about your surroundings, provide information, and assist with supported translation features. Battery life is rated for up to eight hours of typical use, with the included charging case providing additional power throughout the day. Meta’s Black Friday promotion takes 25% off eligible Gen 2 models, bringing the starting price down from $379 to $284.25. The VITURE Luma Ultra is another excellent option for anyone who wants a private virtual display, which is great if gaming and watching movies are high on the priority list. The VITURE Luma Ultra is another excellent option for anyone who wants a private virtual display, particularly if gaming and watching movies are high on the priority list. The glasses also support spatial features, including six-degrees-of-freedom tracking and hand gestures when used with compatible software and accessories. VITURE’s Black Friday sale brings the Luma Ultra down to $449 from $599. Want a more sporty look with the Meta smart glasses tech? Well, you can check out the Oakley Meta HSTN. It combines Oakley’s distinctive eyewear design with the camera, audio, and AI capabilities of Meta’s smart glasses platform. The HSTN features a 12MP camera with 3K video recording, open-ear speakers, and built-in microphones. This makes it great for capturing hands-free footage during walks, outdoor adventures, and other activities where pulling out a smartphone isn’t convenient. There’s also an IPX4 water-resistance rating, providing protection against splashes, sweat, and light rain. Meta advertises up to eight hours of battery life under typical usage conditions, with additional charging available through the included case. With a 25% Black Friday discount, the starting price falls to $299.30, down from $399. It’s a handy alternative to the Ray-Ban models for buyers who prefer Oakley’s styling and sport-oriented lenses. The RayNeo Air 4 Pro is one of the more affordable ways to get a large virtual screen for gaming and entertainment. One of its standout features is HDR10 support, designed to deliver better highlight and shadow detail when viewing compatible content. The glasses use Micro-OLED displays with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. So they are comfortable for gaming. You also get RayNeo’s Vision 4000 processing chip, which supports features such as SDR-to-HDR conversion, along with audio tuned by Bang & Olufsen. There’s compatibility with supported USB-C devices, including smartphones, laptops, and handheld gaming systems. As with most wearable displays, the connected device must support the appropriate video output, or you may need an additional adapter. At a current advertised price of $233.22, down from $299, the Air 4 Pro is one of the least expensive display-equipped glasses in this roundup. The Rokid AI Glasses Style is a little different from the wearable displays in this roundup. Rather than putting a screen in front of your eyes, they’re designed around everyday AI assistance, audio, and hands-free photography. At just 38.5 grams without prescription lenses, they’re also relatively lightweight. Rokid has equipped them with a 12MP Sony camera capable of recording up to 3K video, along with open-ear audio and voice-based AI assistance.
