There are plenty of great options to choose from, which will likely suit the needs of different users. Whether you’re looking to put a massive virtual screen in front of your eyes, record videos without reaching for your phone, or experiment with wearable AI, you have something for everyone.

And the savings aren’t bad, either. XREAL is knocking $100 off its One Pro glasses, VITURE has discounted its Luma Ultra by $150, and Meta is offering 25% off selected Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses. So I’ve narrowed things down to six deals worth checking out, covering everything from gaming and portable entertainment to hands-free photography and AI assistance.

XREAL has a great deal for you if you’re looking to turn any compatible device into a massive personal screen. The XREAL One Pro is a great deal, which basically turns it into a wearable display that lets you enjoy movies, games, and even desktop applications without needing a physical monitor in front of you.
At $499, down from $599, the One Pro is worth considering if you’ve been waiting to try a high-end wearable display.

INAIR Pod is an ideal companion for compatible AR glasses, bringing Android apps and spatial computing to selected models from VITURE, XREAL, and RayNeo. Run supported apps directly on the Pod and create a workspace with up to six virtual windows in supported INAIR configurations. Spatial features and window availability vary by glasses model. Get it for $351.99, down from $439.99 . For an integrated setup, the INAIR 2 Go Pack puts a portable spatial workstation in your bag. It combines INAIR 2 Pro glasses, INAIR Pod, a foldable keyboard, and a carrying case for work and entertainment on the go—from browsing and writing to watching your favorite content. Get the bundle for $799.20, down from $999 .

Ray-Ban Meta glasses are still one of the easiest ways to try smart eyewear without committing to something that looks a little too futuristic. The second-generation models retain Ray-Ban’s familiar styling while adding an upgraded camera, improved battery life, and Meta AI integration.

You get a 12MP camera capable of recording video at up to 3K resolution, along with open-ear speakers and microphones for music, phone calls, and voice commands. Meta AI can also help answer questions about your surroundings, provide information, and assist with supported translation features. Battery life is rated for up to eight hours of typical use, with the included charging case providing additional power throughout the day.
Meta’s Black Friday promotion takes 25% off eligible Gen 2 models, bringing the starting price down from $379 to $284.25.

The VITURE Luma Ultra is another excellent option for anyone who wants a private virtual display, which is great if gaming and watching movies are high on the priority list. The VITURE Luma Ultra is another excellent option for anyone who wants a private virtual display, particularly if gaming and watching movies are high on the priority list.

The glasses also support spatial features, including six-degrees-of-freedom tracking and hand gestures when used with compatible software and accessories. VITURE’s Black Friday sale brings the Luma Ultra down to $449 from $599.

Want a more sporty look with the Meta smart glasses tech? Well, you can check out the Oakley Meta HSTN. It combines Oakley’s distinctive eyewear design with the camera, audio, and AI capabilities of Meta’s smart glasses platform. The HSTN features a 12MP camera with 3K video recording, open-ear speakers, and built-in microphones.

This makes it great for capturing hands-free footage during walks, outdoor adventures, and other activities where pulling out a smartphone isn’t convenient. There’s also an IPX4 water-resistance rating, providing protection against splashes, sweat, and light rain. Meta advertises up to eight hours of battery life under typical usage conditions, with additional charging available through the included case.
With a 25% Black Friday discount, the starting price falls to $299.30, down from $399. It’s a handy alternative to the Ray-Ban models for buyers who prefer Oakley’s styling and sport-oriented lenses.

The RayNeo Air 4 Pro is one of the more affordable ways to get a large virtual screen for gaming and entertainment. One of its standout features is HDR10 support, designed to deliver better highlight and shadow detail when viewing compatible content. The glasses use Micro-OLED displays with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. So they are comfortable for gaming.

You also get RayNeo’s Vision 4000 processing chip, which supports features such as SDR-to-HDR conversion, along with audio tuned by Bang & Olufsen. There’s compatibility with supported USB-C devices, including smartphones, laptops, and handheld gaming systems. As with most wearable displays, the connected device must support the appropriate video output, or you may need an additional adapter.
At a current advertised price of $233.22, down from $299, the Air 4 Pro is one of the least expensive display-equipped glasses in this roundup.

The Rokid AI Glasses Style is a little different from the wearable displays in this roundup. Rather than putting a screen in front of your eyes, they’re designed around everyday AI assistance, audio, and hands-free photography. At just 38.5 grams without prescription lenses, they’re also relatively lightweight. Rokid has equipped them with a 12MP Sony camera capable of recording up to 3K video, along with open-ear audio and voice-based AI assistance.

The glasses can help with supported tasks such as translation, answering questions, and capturing photos or videos from your perspective. They connect to a smartphone through the Hi Rokid app, which also manages supported features and settings. Rokid’s Black Friday deal lists the AI Glasses Style for $279, down from a $399 comparison price. It’s a good choice if you want to try out an AI assistant and camera built into ordinary-looking eyewear rather than watching movies on a virtual screen.

I've tried a bunch of open-ear earbuds over the last couple of years. While I don't personally gravitate towards them, they serve a few specific and useful features. The freedom they offer has its perks, but they aren't always comfortable--at least for me. Some have bulky hooks that wrap around your ears, while others start becoming uncomfortable after a few hours.

So after Xiaomi sent over the new Clip earbuds, along with the Xiaomi 18 Pros, I was really looking forward to how different these feel, and not just how they sound. After all, clip-on earbuds have become pretty popular, and several manufacturers have already experimented with more fashionable designs. And getting the shiny Sand Gold variant, I wasn't expecting people to start asking whether I got my ears pierced.

I buy Echo speakers and Kindles as gifts and keep them for myself, and that is exactly why Amazon's Black Friday sale caught my attention. Below are six picks, starting with the cheapest Amazon Echo product (which, to your surprise, isn't a speaker) and going all the way up to the latest Kindle Scribe Colorsoft, which helps you save $200.

So I’ve narrowed things down to six deals worth checking out, covering everything from gaming and portable entertainment to hands-free photography and AI assistance. XREAL has a great deal for you if you’re looking to turn any compatible device into a massive personal screen. The XREAL One Pro is a great deal, which basically turns it into a wearable display that lets you enjoy movies, games, and even desktop applications without needing a physical monitor in front of you. At $499, down from $599, the One Pro is worth considering if you’ve been waiting to try a high-end wearable display. INAIR Pod is an ideal companion for compatible AR glasses, bringing Android apps and spatial computing to selected models from VITURE, XREAL, and RayNeo. Run supported apps directly on the Pod and create a workspace with up to six virtual windows in supported INAIR configurations. Spatial features and window availability vary by glasses model. Get it for $351.99, down from $439.99 . For an integrated setup, the INAIR 2 Go Pack puts a portable spatial workstation in your bag. It combines INAIR 2 Pro glasses, INAIR Pod, a foldable keyboard, and a carrying case for work and entertainment on the go—from browsing and writing to watching your favorite content. Get the bundle for $799.20, down from $999 . Ray-Ban Meta glasses are still one of the easiest ways to try smart eyewear without committing to something that looks a little too futuristic. The second-generation models retain Ray-Ban’s familiar styling while adding an upgraded camera, improved battery life, and Meta AI integration. You get a 12MP camera capable of recording video at up to 3K resolution, along with open-ear speakers and microphones for music, phone calls, and voice commands. Meta AI can also help answer questions about your surroundings, provide information, and assist with supported translation features. extraction.body: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board? Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world. Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology. From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes. In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist. That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one. It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC. That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ. "The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports". Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island. To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors. On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain. Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics. "Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says. In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025. In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States. For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC. In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation. In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story. Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open." However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better. Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China. Jensen Huang signs a Taiwanese banknote for a visitor at Computex 2026 in Taipei This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment. Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang. Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks. "Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank. Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets. Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat. Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry. "I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said. Additional reporting by Benny Lu, BBC Chinese Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology. From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes. In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist. That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one. It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC. That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ. "The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports". Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island. To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors. On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain. It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics. "Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says. In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025. In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States. But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy. The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added. The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said. For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC. In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation. In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story. Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open." However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better. Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China. Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models. This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment. Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang. Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks. "Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank. Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets. Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat. Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry. "I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC. In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation. The condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds. The disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases. The seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS said the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments. The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations. Aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case. Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end users that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries. The reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC. It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information. The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China. Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported. The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom. Closing 'loopholes' The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes." "Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said. U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute. Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

extraction.body: CNBC reported on November 26, 2026 that Nvidia chip sellers have told neocloud operators, which rent out accelerated computing capacity, they will not supply GPUs if any of the resulting computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, citing two people familiar with the private communications. The condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds. The disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases. The seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS said the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments. The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations. Aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case. Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end users that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries. The reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Under the reported condition, a neocloud’s hardware access depends on the customers its capacity will serve, wherever the data center is located. sources.title: Nvidia sellers seek buyers after US restrictions on China — CNBC - UA.NEWS
passages: In the United States, sellers of Nvidia graphics processing units are seeking new buyers after rules were tightened restricting remote access by China-linked companies to advanced computing power for artificial intelligence.
CNBC reports that an unusually large volume of offers to sell Nvidia GPUs appeared on the market after the new measures were announced.
According to three CNBC sources, the increase in the number of GPUs put up for sale is directly linked to the new rule.
These restrictions effectively prohibit the direct sale to China of Nvidia's most advanced chips, but Chinese companies could access them remotely through data centers abroad.
Nvidia declined to comment, while the Bureau of Industry and Security did not respond to CNBC's request.
During a third-quarter earnings call on November 17, Nvidia's then acting CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the new restrictions.
At the same time, she expected Nvidia's performance to remain strong, as demand for chips significantly exceeds supply.

extraction.body: In the United States, sellers of Nvidia graphics processing units are seeking new buyers after rules were tightened restricting remote access by China-linked companies to advanced computing power for artificial intelligence. CNBC reports that an unusually large volume of offers to sell Nvidia GPUs appeared on the market after the new measures were announced. The Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Department of Commerce announced an interim final rule on November 16, which took effect on November 19. It restricts certain operating arrangements at foreign data centers under which China-linked customers can obtain significant volumes of advanced computing power. The new restrictions are part of tighter controls on the circumvention of export restrictions. These restrictions effectively prohibit the direct sale to China of Nvidia's most advanced chips, but Chinese companies could access them remotely through data centers abroad. According to three CNBC sources, the increase in the number of GPUs put up for sale is directly linked to the new rule. Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, said that one company directly explained its intention to sell Nvidia chips by citing the new US restrictions. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Two sources who wished to remain anonymous said that sellers are likely trying to dispose of chips initially intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access to computing. Duhamel and one source also reported offers to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced products. Nvidia declined to comment, while the Bureau of Industry and Security did not respond to CNBC's request. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new rules are intended to close loopholes, including the possibility of indirect access to advanced chips through data centers in third countries. During a third-quarter earnings call on November 17, Nvidia's then acting CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the new restrictions. At the same time, she expected Nvidia's performance to remain strong, as demand for chips significantly exceeds supply.

Every GPU that powers a model training cluster has to be built somewhere, and that somewhere is almost always a fab operated by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM). Taiwan Semi does not design the artificial intelligence (AI) chips that get the headlines. Instead, the company manufactures them at nodes no one else can reliably hit at scale. That quiet competitive advantage has turned TSMC into the physical backbone of the AI infrastructure buildout. Nevertheless, the conversation still seems to start and end with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD), or Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). The foundry that is actually printing the silicon rarely gets the same amount of airtime. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » This gap is strange once you understand how the AI chip stack works. While designers continue to fight over architecture and software, the constraint that decides how many of those designs actually ship is advanced-node capacity -- and TSMC owns most of that market. Nvidia and AMD design GPUs while Micron builds memory solutions layered alongside these chips. None of these companies do all of the manufacturing work to bring their products to life, however. TSMC holds roughly 73% of the pure-play foundry market as measured by revenue and reportedly closer to 90% of the market for the most advanced nodes. For years, Apple was credited as TSMC's largest customer. However, Nvidia took over that title earlier this year. This shift directly tracks the AI infrastructure cycle. High-performance computing, the area that covers AI accelerators and related server silicon, has become Taiwan Semi's core growth engine. The company's management points to AI-accelerator revenue compounding in the mid-to-high 50% range through the end of the decade, and lifted its longer-term company revenue growth outlook toward at least 25%. While competition from Samsung and Intel exist, both companies are spending heavily on scaling foundry operations and neither company is yet to close the gap on the yield and volume at nodes Nvidia and AMD actually need for current and next-generation accelerators. TSMC's financial growth supports the idea that the AI infrastructure supercycle is more than a temporary surge. Full-year 2025 revenue reached about $122 billion, up nearly 36% year over year. Meanwhile, gross margin climbed to 60% from 56% percent the year before. Through the first half of 2026, Taiwan Semi's revenue grew 37% year over year to $76.1 billion while while gross margin expanded into the mid-60% range, underscoring the level of pricing power the company commands right now. The company is also spending heavily on capital expenditures (capex) to help stay ahead of demand. Rising infrastructure spend might look expensive in any single year, but over a multi-year AI buildout it is what keeps the company's moat intact. Customers cannot easily dual-source manufacturing for leading edge nodes. This makes Taiwan Semi's revenue and profit tailwinds tied to the duration of the infrastructure supercycle itself rather than to one specific product launch. The chart below illustrates how investors are treating TSMC as a picks-and-shovels name that should trade at a discount to some of the primary chip designers. Trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) puts the stock near 34 times, which looks rich upon first glance. But on a forward P/E basis, Taiwan Semi is a different story. While the company's forward P/E of 28 is not a deep-value multiple per se, it is also not stretched against a company still expected to grow revenue by a high double-digit percent range and compound earnings as margins hold. Nvidia and AMD capture more of the narrative premium because their products are visible. For the time being, Micron will ride the memory upcycle that AI also requires. Taiwan Semi sits underneath all of them. While geopolitical risk around Taiwan is an obvious factor to consider, in addition to the cost of building fabs here in the U.S., they do not erase a foundry position that remains the hardest part of the AI supply chain to replicate. On a forward earnings valuation basis, I think TSMC stock still looks like a strong candidate to buy and hold throughout the AI infrastructure era. While competition from Samsung and Intel exist, both companies are spending heavily on scaling foundry operations and neither company is yet to close the gap on the yield and volume at nodes Nvidia and AMD actually need for current and next-generation accelerators.

TSMC's financial growth supports the idea that the AI infrastructure supercycle is more than a temporary surge. Full-year 2025 revenue reached about $122 billion, up nearly 36% year over year. Meanwhile, gross margin climbed to 60% from 56% percent the year before. Through the first half of 2026, Taiwan Semi's revenue grew 37% year over year to $76.1 billion while while gross margin expanded into the mid-60% range, underscoring the level of pricing power the company commands right now.

The company is also spending heavily on capital expenditures (capex) to help stay ahead of demand. Rising infrastructure spend might look expensive in any single year, but over a multi-year AI buildout it is what keeps the company's moat intact. Customers cannot easily dual-source manufacturing for leading edge nodes. This makes Taiwan Semi's revenue and profit tailwinds tied to the duration of the infrastructure supercycle itself rather than to one specific product launch.

The chart below illustrates how investors are treating TSMC as a picks-and-shovels name that should trade at a discount to some of the primary chip designers. Trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) puts the stock near 34 times, which looks rich upon first glance. But on a forward P/E basis, Taiwan Semi is a different story. While the company's forward P/E of 28 is not a deep-value multiple per se, it is also not stretched against a company still expected to grow revenue by a high double-digit percent range and compound earnings as margins hold.

Nvidia and AMD capture more of the narrative premium because their products are visible. For the time being, Micron will ride the memory upcycle that AI also requires. Taiwan Semi sits underneath all of them.

While geopolitical risk around Taiwan is an obvious factor to consider, in addition to the cost of building fabs here in the U.S., they do not erase a foundry position that remains the hardest part of the AI supply chain to replicate. On a forward earnings valuation basis, I think TSMC stock still looks like a strong candidate to buy and hold throughout the AI infrastructure era.

By Adam Spatacco – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:54PM EST 10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing › For much of the last four years, semiconductor stocks have been some of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. While Nvidia ( NVDA -3.91% ) has become the king of AI accelerators, Micron Technology ( MU -4.53% ) is capitalizing on unprecedented demand for memory chips. Although both companies have attractive long-term growth prospects, competition could complicate their investment narratives over the next several years. Moreover, as the AI infrastructure landscape evolves, identifying which chip architectures will dominate the market is becoming more challenging. Fortunately, there's one semiconductor company that stands to benefit from virtually every major development across the AI chip landscape: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM -1.96% ) . Between its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking equipment, and CUDA software ecosystem, Nvidia has an exceptionally durable competitive moat. Nevertheless, Advanced Micro Devices is investing aggressively in its Instinct accelerator portfolio, while some of Nvidia's largest customers are developing custom silicon. Broadcom has emerged as an important partner in the market for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), most notably through its relationship with Alphabet and its tensor processing units (TPUs). Meanwhile, Microsoft and Amazon are also developing their own chip portfolios, including Maia, Trainium, and Inferentia. Another potential source of competition is Space Exploration Technologies ' collaboration with Intel on Terafab. Terafab is Elon Musk's semiconductor manufacturing initiative that could eventually reduce SpaceX's dependence on third-party chip suppliers. Although commercial-scale production remains uncertain, the project underscores a growing appetite for vertically integrated semiconductor solutions. Micron faces a different set of challenges. While the proliferation of generative AI has ushered in a memory supercycle, memory-intensive applications such as humanoid robotics and autonomous vehicles should introduce additional tailwinds over the next several years. However, Micron competes against Samsung and SK Hynix in the high bandwidth memory (HBM) market. Furthermore, memory pricing has historically been cyclical, leaving producers vulnerable to fluctuations in supply, demand, and profitability. While Nvidia and Micron could both continue thriving, there is an alternative way to invest in the semiconductor industry without betting on a particular chip designer or memory manufacturer. Unlike Nvidia and AMD, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) primarily manufactures semiconductors designed by other companies. Its customer base includes businesses spanning GPUs, custom AI accelerators, smartphone processors, and automotive chips. Against this backdrop, if Nvidia continues to dominate the AI accelerator market, TSMC benefits. Should AMD start to capture additional market share or custom ASICs become increasingly popular, TSMC still stands to benefit because it manufactures chips across these competing architectures as well. Interestingly, Taiwan Semi also has exposure to the memory supercycle. While the company isn't a producer of conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), its collaboration with SK Hynix involves manufacturing logic base dies for next-generation HBM4 solutions. Moreover, TSMC's advanced packaging technologies -- particularly its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) platform -- play a critical role in integrating AI processors with HBM. As a result, growing demand for more sophisticated memory configurations creates additional markets for TSMC beyond traditional wafer fabrication. The most compelling aspect of TSMC's competitive positioning is the sheer magnitude of its market share. Industry estimates suggest that Taiwan Semi controls roughly 73% of the global pure-play foundry market . By contrast, the next closest competitor sits at just 6%. Although TSMC isn't technically a monopoly, its dominance gives it the characteristics of one. The company's manufacturing expertise, technological edge, production scale, and customer relationships are simply too difficult for the competition to replicate at scale. During the third quarter, Taiwan Semi generated $46.7 billion in revenue, representing 41% year-over-year growth. Meanwhile, the company's gross margin reached nearly 65%, and its operating margin expanded to about 59%. Management expects revenue to reach $53.3 billion in the fourth quarter, implying 58% year-over-year growth. These results illustrate how TSMC's manufacturing scale is translating insatiable semiconductor demand into robust profitability. Despite these impressive financial trends, Taiwan Semi stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 15.7. That valuation profile looks attractive for a business generating this level of growth and profitability while commanding such a dominant market position. Rather than attempting to identify which chip designer or memory producer will emerge victorious over the next several years, investing in the company that manufactures many of the industry's most in-demand products looks like a compelling strategy. TSMC's architecture-agnostic business model, durable competitive advantages, and reasonable valuation make it a compelling semiconductor stock to buy now and hold through the end of the decade. Every GPU that powers a model training cluster has to be built somewhere, and that somewhere is almost always a fab operated by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM). Taiwan Semi does not design the artificial intelligence (AI) chips that get the headlines. Instead, the company manufactures them at nodes no one else can reliably hit at scale. That quiet competitive advantage has turned TSMC into the physical backbone of the AI infrastructure buildout. Nevertheless, the conversation still seems to start and end with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD), or Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). The foundry that is actually printing the silicon rarely gets the same amount of airtime. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » This gap is strange once you understand how the AI chip stack works. While designers continue to fight over architecture and software, the constraint that decides how many of those designs actually ship is advanced-node capacity -- and TSMC owns most of that market. Nvidia and AMD design GPUs while Micron builds memory solutions layered alongside these chips. None of these companies do all of the manufacturing work to bring their products to life, however. TSMC holds roughly 73% of the pure-play foundry market as measured by revenue and reportedly closer to 90% of the market for the most advanced nodes. For years, Apple was credited as TSMC's largest customer. However, Nvidia took over that title earlier this year. This shift directly tracks the AI infrastructure cycle. High-performance computing, the area that covers AI accelerators and related server silicon, has become Taiwan Semi's core growth engine. The company's management points to AI-accelerator revenue compounding in the mid-to-high 50% range through the end of the decade, and lifted its longer-term company revenue growth outlook toward at least 25%. While competition from Samsung and Intel exist, both companies are spending heavily on scaling foundry operations and neither company is yet to close the gap on the yield and volume at nodes Nvidia and AMD actually need for current and next-generation accelerators. TSMC's financial growth supports the idea that the AI infrastructure supercycle is more than a temporary surge. Full-year 2025 revenue reached about $122 billion, up nearly 36% year over year. Meanwhile, gross margin climbed to 60% from 56% percent the year before. Through the first half of 2026, Taiwan Semi's revenue grew 37% year over year to $76.1 billion while while gross margin expanded into the mid-60% range, underscoring the level of pricing power the company commands right now. The company is also spending heavily on capital expenditures (capex) to help stay ahead of demand. Rising infrastructure spend might look expensive in any single year, but over a multi-year AI buildout it is what keeps the company's moat intact. Customers cannot easily dual-source manufacturing for leading edge nodes. This makes Taiwan Semi's revenue and profit tailwinds tied to the duration of the infrastructure supercycle itself rather than to one specific product launch. The chart below illustrates how investors are treating TSMC as a picks-and-shovels name that should trade at a discount to some of the primary chip designers. Trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) puts the stock near 34 times, which looks rich upon first glance. But on a forward P/E basis, Taiwan Semi is a different story. While the company's forward P/E of 28 is not a deep-value multiple per se, it is also not stretched against a company still expected to grow revenue by a high double-digit percent range and compound earnings as margins hold. Nvidia and AMD capture more of the narrative premium because their products are visible. For the time being, Micron will ride the memory upcycle that AI also requires. Taiwan Semi sits underneath all of them. While geopolitical risk around Taiwan is an obvious factor to consider, in addition to the cost of building fabs here in the U.S., they do not erase a foundry position that remains the hardest part of the AI supply chain to replicate. On a forward earnings valuation basis, I think TSMC stock still looks like a strong candidate to buy and hold throughout the AI infrastructure era. Nvidia is the undisputed king in the AI accelerator market thanks to its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking technology, and CUDA software ecosystem. However, the company's largest customers are developing alternatives. Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta Platforms are investing in application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) optimized for their own AI workloads. While these chips won't replace Nvidia's GPUs entirely, they should reduce dependence on Nvidia while giving the hyperscalers more control over infrastructure costs and model performance. Meanwhile, Nvidia is also exploring agentic AI , autonomous vehicles, and robotics. Indeed, these opportunities could be enormous. But commercial adoption may take longer than the next four years. Micron is looking at a different challenge. The company's memory solutions are essential for AI computing, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM. Memory manufacturing has historically been a cyclical industry, meaning today's shortages and elevated prices will lead producers to expand capacity. By next decade, more supply should come online, leading to pricing pressure and eroding profit margins. Moreover, competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) also deserves attention. Although CXMT is not yet an equivalent competitor across every advanced memory category, its progress could affect the industry's supply dynamics over time. Here's what makes TSMC different: Whether AI hyperscalers buy Nvidia GPUs, develop custom silicon, or adopt entirely new architectures, many of those chips will require Taiwan Semi's advanced foundry capabilities. In turn, Taiwan Semi doesn't need Nvidia to defeat Alphabet's custom chip strategy. It can manufacture chips for both companies. Meanwhile, TSMC delivered a gross margin of 66.4% and an operating margin of 58.7%. This underscores the pricing power commanded by the company's advanced manufacturing technology. Management expects AI-driven momentum to continue. For Q4, revenue is projected to reach between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion as the company's next-generation, 2-nanometer technology continues ramping. Building a semiconductor foundry requires significant upfront capital, years of engineering development, and the ability to manufacture complex chips at commercially viable yields. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) faces growing competition from custom silicon developed by its own customers. Meanwhile, Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) could face less favorable memory market dynamics as manufacturers expand production.

Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

This is why I see Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) , otherwise known as TSMC, as a more attractive long-term opportunity. Taiwan Semi's latest earnings report displayed how its business is becoming more valuable than ever to the AI infrastructure era.

Nvidia is the undisputed king in the AI accelerator market thanks to its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking technology, and CUDA software ecosystem. However, the company's largest customers are developing alternatives. Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta Platforms are investing in application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) optimized for their own AI workloads. While these chips won't replace Nvidia's GPUs entirely, they should reduce dependence on Nvidia while giving the hyperscalers more control over infrastructure costs and model performance.
Meanwhile, Nvidia is also exploring agentic AI , autonomous vehicles, and robotics. Indeed, these opportunities could be enormous. But commercial adoption may take longer than the next four years.

Micron is looking at a different challenge. The company's memory solutions are essential for AI computing, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM. Memory manufacturing has historically been a cyclical industry, meaning today's shortages and elevated prices will lead producers to expand capacity. By next decade, more supply should come online, leading to pricing pressure and eroding profit margins.

Moreover, competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) also deserves attention. Although CXMT is not yet an equivalent competitor across every advanced memory category, its progress could affect the industry's supply dynamics over time.

Here's what makes TSMC different: Whether AI hyperscalers buy Nvidia GPUs, develop custom silicon, or adopt entirely new architectures, many of those chips will require Taiwan Semi's advanced foundry capabilities. In turn, Taiwan Semi doesn't need Nvidia to defeat Alphabet's custom chip strategy. It can manufacture chips for both companies.

Taiwan Semi's third-quarter earnings report put the company's competitive position on full display. The company generated $46.7 billion in revenue, representing 41% growth year over year. Meanwhile, TSMC delivered a gross margin of 66.4% and an operating margin of 58.7%. This underscores the pricing power commanded by the company's advanced manufacturing technology.

Management expects AI-driven momentum to continue. For Q4, revenue is projected to reach between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion as the company's next-generation, 2-nanometer technology continues ramping.

Building a semiconductor foundry requires significant upfront capital, years of engineering development, and the ability to manufacture complex chips at commercially viable yields. This creates substantial barriers to entry. As demand for AI compute grows, TSMC should benefit from higher production volumes, more sophisticated manufacturing processes, and additional opportunities in advanced packaging.

Furthermore, the company's opportunities extend beyond today's AI hardware. Consider what could happen between now and 2030. AI workloads are going to shift from training large language models (LLMs) toward inference deployments across autonomous systems, robotics, and applications that have not yet been commercialized at scale. Some of these will require more GPUs, while others will depend on custom accelerators, central processing units (CPUs), or specialized processors.

While TSMC doesn't manufacture DRAM or HBM, it does produce advanced logic chips that operate alongside these memory types. In other words, Taiwan Semi stands to benefit from the broader evolution of AI rather than relying on one particular semiconductor category.

That versatility potentially supports more valuation expansion for Taiwan Semi relative to other semiconductor stocks. Historically, chip manufacturers traded at discounts relative to other designers due to their capital-intensive business models. However, TSMC's dominant position in leading-edge manufacturing, growing profitability, and indispensable role in the AI infrastructure value chain could justify a higher earnings multiple in the long-run.

To me, Taiwan Semi offers a unique proposition: exposure to a broad range of advanced chip architectures regardless of which designers are in demand. Combined with its manufacturing capabilities, robust profitability, and potential for long-term upside, I see TSMC as a compelling buy-and-hold AI chip stock through 2030.

Moreover, as the AI infrastructure landscape evolves, identifying which chip architectures will dominate the market is becoming more challenging. Fortunately, there's one semiconductor company that stands to benefit from virtually every major development across the AI chip landscape: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM -1.96% ) . Between its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking equipment, and CUDA software ecosystem, Nvidia has an exceptionally durable competitive moat. Nevertheless, Advanced Micro Devices is investing aggressively in its Instinct accelerator portfolio, while some of Nvidia's largest customers are developing custom silicon. Broadcom has emerged as an important partner in the market for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), most notably through its relationship with Alphabet and its tensor processing units (TPUs). Meanwhile, Microsoft and Amazon are also developing their own chip portfolios, including Maia, Trainium, and Inferentia. Another potential source of competition is Space Exploration Technologies ' collaboration with Intel on Terafab. Terafab is Elon Musk's semiconductor manufacturing initiative that could eventually reduce SpaceX's dependence on third-party chip suppliers. Although commercial-scale production remains uncertain, the project underscores a growing appetite for vertically integrated semiconductor solutions. Micron faces a different set of challenges. While the proliferation of generative AI has ushered in a memory supercycle, memory-intensive applications such as humanoid robotics and autonomous vehicles should introduce additional tailwinds over the next several years. However, Micron competes against Samsung and SK Hynix in the high bandwidth memory (HBM) market. Furthermore, memory pricing has historically been cyclical, leaving producers vulnerable to fluctuations in supply, demand, and profitability. While Nvidia and Micron could both continue thriving, there is an alternative way to invest in the semiconductor industry without betting on a particular chip designer or memory manufacturer. Unlike Nvidia and AMD, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) primarily manufactures semiconductors designed by other companies. Its customer base includes businesses spanning GPUs, custom AI accelerators, smartphone processors, and automotive chips. Against this backdrop, if Nvidia continues to dominate the AI accelerator market, TSMC benefits. Should AMD start to capture additional market share or custom ASICs become increasingly popular, TSMC still stands to benefit because it manufactures chips across these competing architectures as well. Interestingly, Taiwan Semi also has exposure to the memory supercycle. While the company isn't a producer of conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), its collaboration with SK Hynix involves manufacturing logic base dies for next-generation HBM4 solutions. Moreover, TSMC's advanced packaging technologies -- particularly its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) platform -- play a critical role in integrating AI processors with HBM. As a result, growing demand for more sophisticated memory configurations creates additional markets for TSMC beyond traditional wafer fabrication. The most compelling aspect of TSMC's competitive positioning is the sheer magnitude of its market share. Industry estimates suggest that Taiwan Semi controls roughly 73% of the global pure-play foundry market . By contrast, the next closest competitor sits at just 6%. Although TSMC isn't technically a monopoly, its dominance gives it the characteristics of one. The company's manufacturing expertise, technological edge, production scale, and customer relationships are simply too difficult for the competition to replicate at scale. Management expects revenue to reach $53.3 billion in the fourth quarter, implying 58% year-over-year growth. Despite these impressive financial trends, Taiwan Semi stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 15.7. That valuation profile looks attractive for a business generating this level of growth and profitability while commanding such a dominant market position. Rather than attempting to identify which chip designer or memory producer will emerge victorious over the next several years, investing in the company that manufactures many of the industry's most in-demand products looks like a compelling strategy. extraction.body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. extraction.body: ChatGPT users working with GPT-6.2 will now run into their usage limits sooner. OpenAI says it made a billing mistake when it launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, one that "incorrectly discounted" usage of both models for most users. Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced the fix on X on November 26. From now on, "the same work will use more of your plan's usage allowance." Compared with the previous week, users will reach their limits 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol. Other models were not affected, and OpenAI will not charge for the difference on past usage. Astra and Sol have been available in ChatGPT Work and Codex since November 17. A version of Sol has also powered the regular Chat tab for Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise since November 23. Sottiaux only refers to the plan's usage allowance and does not say whether message limits in the Chat tab change as well. Free users have no access to either model, so nothing changes for them. extraction.body: Bogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century." Nesvit is the co-founder of microseries app My Drama, built around the latest, bite-sized form of storytelling. Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year. They often feature romantic tropes and typically end in cliffhangers to keep viewers hooked. The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms. The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024. "It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said. Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps. TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data. Startups DramaBox and ReelShort beat out entertainment giants Netflix and Disney in average mobile usage time in the U.S. in the third quarter, according to Sensor Tower. As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in. Fox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas. The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025. Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app. Thus far, hits include dark academia series "Secret Society: Till Blood Do Us Part" and "Kiss of the Pirate King." Individual series have reached tens of millions of views, according to the company. Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience. Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit. "One of the exciting things that we learned when we started talking to studios in Hollywood around two years ago is that all of them are super hungry for consumer data," Nesvit said. "They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content." Nesvit said the company will provide studios with feedback on everything from the length of a camera shot to what color dress a character should wear. "Our goal is how we can drive audiences from YouTube, from TikTok, from Instagram to our platform, and also create those kinds of synergies [with] legacy media," he said. Holywater recently adapted Season 3 of Fox's reality TV hit "Farmer Wants a Wife" into a microseries fit for the platform. The company also plans to create a scripted series featuring 30 three-minute episodes inspired by Fox's "Fear Factor: House of Fear." Holywater currently relies on a combination of subscription fees, which make up about 80% of its revenue, and money from advertisers. Nesvit said the company is also exploring incorporating brand integrations. The company is already profitable, its co-founders said. "You attract organically the audience that loves that [intellectual property]," he said. While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house. Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun, who have collectively held leadership roles at NBCUniversal, Showtime, Warner Bros. Discovery and ABC, have jointly founded a microdrama startup called aTwist. "One of the specialties that we have is really what it means to be a great storyteller," Rovner told CNBC in an interview. "I was president of Warner Bros. Television. I was there for 22 years. During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest." "A lot of our competitors' completion rates are very low, their churn rates are very high," Rovner said. "They can often bring people into the store but they can't keep them." The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data. The market intelligence firm notes that the number of users lost in each quarter this year has roughly equaled the number of users gained. CandyJar, a two year-old platform that releases a new romance about once a week, is on track to generate more than $100 million in annual sales. According to its executives, each microdrama series typically spans 50 to 75 episodes, and takes about three months to produce at a cost of between $100,000 to $300,000. A typical half-hour sitcom costs between $2 million and $4 million per episode.CandyJar’s ”romance-forward” platform attracts a 99.9% female audience, said Elana Zeltser, director of creative development for Inkitt CandyJar. Television, said they’re using everything they learned about how to quickly hook a television audience. A commercial gig followed by work as an extra, then getting an agent before booking that sitcom, and then, for the lucky few, a successful career. But that arc has changed, according to Hernan Lopez, the head of Owl, who was previously president and CEO of Fox International.“Today, you hear anecdotally of many people coming to L.A. and getting their first job through a vertical drama.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience.
Fox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas.
The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025.
Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app.
The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data.
NBCUniversal's Peacock launched its own vertical video channel within the app this summer that features both original unscripted series and more traditional vertical dramas .
Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year.
As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in.
During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest."
Despite the flurry of investment, Hollywood still faces the challenge of how to translate viewing hours into profit, especially for shorter content.
"They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content."
While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house.
Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit.
