sources.title: Data Centers Are Driving a US Gas Boom
passages: But this new demand for natural gas from data centers is coming right as the Trump administration is rolling back regulations on the industry.
sources.body: But this new demand for natural gas from data centers is coming right as the Trump administration is rolling back regulations on the industry.

extraction.body: The findings from Global Energy Monitor, a San Francisco–based nonprofit that tracks oil and gas developments, come as the Trump administration is both encouraging data center build-out and doing away with pollution regulations on power plants and oil and gas extraction. They will also almost certainly mean an increase in US greenhouse gas emissions, even if some of the projects tracked by Global Energy Monitor never get built. “The implications are huge when you’re talking about this size of a build-out,” says Jonathan Banks, a senior climate adviser at Clean Air Task Force, a nonprofit that works to reduce emissions. (Clean Air Task Force was not involved in the Global Energy Monitor research.) Building all the gas-fired power infrastructure that was in development at the end of last year could increase the US gas fleet by nearly 50 percent, according to Global Energy Monitor’s findings. If all the projects in the development pipeline are built, it would add almost 252 gigawatts of gas power to the US fleet. (Estimates vary, but 1 gigawatt can power up to a million homes, depending on the energy use of the region.) Data centers have helped to nearly triple the demand for gas-fired power in the US over the past two years. When Global Energy Monitor last released its tracker, in early 2024, it logged around 85 gigawatts of gas-fired power in the development pipeline in the US. Just over 4 gigawatts of that development were explicitly earmarked for data centers. But in 2025, more than 97 gigawatts of demand tracked were from projects that will be used to power data centers—almost 25 times higher than the 2024 figures. “About a year and a half ago, we started to see this increase in proposals for data centers specifically,” says Jenny Martos, a research analyst at Global Energy Monitor who worked on the report. To put together the research, Global Energy Monitor reviewed publicly available sources of data on gas power build-outs in the pipeline. These include state-level regulatory filings, air quality permits, and public announcements from companies. (Martos says that the group compared its findings with industry-held data as a benchmark.) As the data center build-out continues across the country, developers are scrambling to secure power from any and all sources—and utilities are racing to meet the projected demand. This has meant that dirtier power sources are getting a second shot at staying online: coal-fired power plants around the country have recently been given extensions on their retirement dates, boosted by coal-friendly policies from the Trump administration. Natural gas is a much cleaner power option than coal-fired power, but gas plants do release CO2 emissions. About 35 percent of US energy-related CO2 emissions in 2022 came from burning natural gas. “Gas is cleaner when burnt than coal, but when you're talking about this much gas, you're talking about a lot of CO2 associated with it, too,” says Banks. A larger concern with natural gas is methane leaks during the extraction process. Methane stays for a shorter period of time in the atmosphere than CO2, but it is 80 times more potent over a 20 year period. Climate scientists say that decreasing methane emissions over the shorter term is crucial to controlling climate change in the long run. It’s estimated that oil and gas production accounts for a third of all global methane leaks; the US is the largest producer of natural gas in the world. “If you zero out the methane, and you have a very efficient natural-gas-fired power plant, it is dramatically cleaner than a coal-fired power plant,” says Banks. “But when you layer on the methane emissions, that's when you see those gaps begin to close between coal and natural gas.” A well-regulated oil and gas industry that does its best to stop leaks could go a long way in stopping methane emissions. But this new demand for natural gas from data centers is coming right as the Trump administration is rolling back regulations on the industry. The figures collected by Global Energy Monitor include potential gas units added to a larger grid in order to bolster electricity supply in regions seeing increased demand from data centers. But they also include on-site gas turbines that will solely be used to power data centers. Building power sources on-site, like gas turbines or solar arrays, is becoming increasingly popular for data center developers, who, in some places, are facing yearslong waits to connect to the larger power grid. It’s unlikely that all of the projects tracked by Global Energy Monitor will actually be built. Many data center developers shop around for power with multiple utilities, which helps to inflate overall demand; simply because a data center project has been announced does not mean that it will eventually be built. Efficiency improvements in both data center construction and in AI training will likely decrease some of the projected demand for energy over the next couple of years. A worldwide shortage of gas turbines also will play a big role in determining what actually gets built on time: Two-thirds of the projects tracked worldwide by the Global Energy Monitor do not yet have turbine manufacturers attached to them. “We’re in that phase where we're seeing the explosion in proposals,” Martos says. “What materializes is yet to be determined.” Even just a partial build-out of these facilities would be significant. passages: The findings from Global Energy Monitor, a San Francisco–based nonprofit that tracks oil and gas developments, come as the Trump administration is both encouraging data center build-out and doing away with pollution regulations on power plants and oil and gas extraction.
They will also almost certainly mean an increase in US greenhouse gas emissions, even if some of the projects tracked by Global Energy Monitor never get built.

“The implications are huge when you’re talking about this size of a build-out,” says Jonathan Banks, a senior climate adviser at Clean Air Task Force, a nonprofit that works to reduce emissions. (Clean Air Task Force was not involved in the Global Energy Monitor research.) Building all the gas-fired power infrastructure that was in development at the end of last year could increase the US gas fleet by nearly 50 percent, according to Global Energy Monitor’s findings.

If all the projects in the development pipeline are built, it would add almost 252 gigawatts of gas power to the US fleet. (Estimates vary, but 1 gigawatt can power up to a million homes, depending on the energy use of the region.) Data centers have helped to nearly triple the demand for gas-fired power in the US over the past two years.
When Global Energy Monitor last released its tracker, in early 2024, it logged around 85 gigawatts of gas-fired power in the development pipeline in the US.
Just over 4 gigawatts of that development were explicitly earmarked for data centers.
But in 2025, more than 97 gigawatts of demand tracked were from projects that will be used to power data centers—almost 25 times higher than the 2024 figures.
“About a year and a half ago, we started to see this increase in proposals for data centers specifically,” says Jenny Martos, a research analyst at Global Energy Monitor who worked on the report.
To put together the research, Global Energy Monitor reviewed publicly available sources of data on gas power build-outs in the pipeline.

These include state-level regulatory filings, air quality permits, and public announcements from companies. (Martos says that the group compared its findings with industry-held data as a benchmark.) As the data center build-out continues across the country, developers are scrambling to secure power from any and all sources—and utilities are racing to meet the projected demand.

This has meant that dirtier power sources are getting a second shot at staying online: coal-fired power plants around the country have recently been given extensions on their retirement dates, boosted by coal-friendly policies from the Trump administration.
Natural gas is a much cleaner power option than coal-fired power, but gas plants do release CO2 emissions.
About 35 percent of US energy-related CO2 emissions in 2022 came from burning natural gas.
“Gas is cleaner when burnt than coal, but when you're talking about this much gas, you're talking about a lot of CO2 associated with it, too,” says Banks.
A larger concern with natural gas is methane leaks during the extraction process.
Methane stays for a shorter period of time in the atmosphere than CO2, but it is 80 times more potent over a 20 year period.
Climate scientists say that decreasing methane emissions over the shorter term is crucial to controlling climate change in the long run.
It’s estimated that oil and gas production accounts for a third of all global methane leaks; the US is the largest producer of natural gas in the world.
“If you zero out the methane, and you have a very efficient natural-gas-fired power plant, it is dramatically cleaner than a coal-fired power plant,” says Banks.

“But when you layer on the methane emissions, that's when you see those gaps begin to close between coal and natural gas.” A well-regulated oil and gas industry that does its best to stop leaks could go a long way in stopping methane emissions.
But this new demand for natural gas from data centers is coming right as the Trump administration is rolling back regulations on the industry.
The figures collected by Global Energy Monitor include potential gas units added to a larger grid in order to bolster electricity supply in regions seeing increased demand from data centers.
But they also include on-site gas turbines that will solely be used to power data centers.

Building power sources on-site, like gas turbines or solar arrays, is becoming increasingly popular for data center developers, who, in some places, are facing yearslong waits to connect to the larger power grid.
It’s unlikely that all of the projects tracked by Global Energy Monitor will actually be built.

Many data center developers shop around for power with multiple utilities, which helps to inflate overall demand; simply because a data center project has been announced does not mean that it will eventually be built.

extraction.body: Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation. In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right. Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence. Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today. But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants. If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue. PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand. This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there. And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation. This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead. It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source. But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025. There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high. Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom. This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

sources.title: New Study: Data Centers Are Lowering American’s Electricity Bills and Natural Gas Is Powering the Boom - Energy In Depth
passages: As Energy in Depth has previously analyzed , a recent International Energy Agency study found that for the United States to be able to host a majority (75 percent) of AI computing domestically, it will need to make around 51 gigawatts of electricity available to data centers by 2027.
Natural gas, sourced from Appalachia, the Permian and Haynesville regions, can scale quickly and affordably to keep durable new supply flowing to the grid as data centers grow.
Policymakers are moving to get this new demand onto the grid quickly, while keeping costs fair for families.
On June 18, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Chairman Laura Swett directed six regional grid operators to justify or update their rules for how data centers and other large loads connect.
Swett framed the action around “fair cost allocation, unprecedented transparency for the American ratepayer and speed to power.”
Gas already generates about 41 percent of U.S. electricity, the single largest source on the grid, and it is dispatchable, reliable and affordable, making it the natural choice to power the AI boom.
Data centers have not been driving up electricity bills, according to a new working paper from researchers at the Electric Power Research Initiative (EPRI).
In fact, EPRI estimates that data centers pushed average U.S. residential electricity rates down between 2015 and 2024.
The power system carries enormous fixed costs, so spreading those costs across more electricity sales lowers the average price per kilowatt-hour.

extraction.body: Data centers have not been driving up electricity bills, according to a new working paper from researchers at the Electric Power Research Initiative (EPRI). In fact, EPRI estimates that data centers pushed average U.S. residential electricity rates down between 2015 and 2024. As data centers have multiplied, some communities have raised concerns that the new demand could raise household bills, but the data tells a more encouraging story, one with real life implications for how the country powers the AI boom. According to EPRI’s study , for every 10 percent increase in data center capacity there was a 0.4 percent drop in residential electricity rates. However, the study’s causal estimate runs larger, meaning that for the average residential customer who lived in a state where data center capacity grew 160 percent from 2019 to 2024, rates fell about 6 percent. The reason is straightforward. The power system carries enormous fixed costs, so spreading those costs across more electricity sales lowers the average price per kilowatt-hour. Data centers supply large, steady, long-term demand. That demand also anchors investment in new transmission, distribution, and generation, and because newer equipment runs cheaper and more efficiently than the aging assets it replaces, the whole system becomes more affordable. At the same time, data centers are helping to build a smarter, more reliable grid. Many major operators have committed to financing and accelerating major grid modernization with new substations, transmission upgrades, and more. This benefits entire communities and helps bring down costs across the board. The states hosting the most load bear this out. In Virginia, where data centers now draw over 20 percent of the state’s electricity, rate increases tracked right in line with the national average. California, by contrast, saw prices climb nearly 40 percent, driven largely by wildfire costs, infrastructure constraints, and state policies, rather than data center farms. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce recently found the same conclusion in an analysis of recent 2025 electricity prices. While rapid growth in data centers and manufacturing has increased electricity demand, the state data shows that this increased demand does not equate to higher prices, rather individual policy and access to infrastructure are the driving forces behind regional price disparities. Policymakers are moving to get this new demand onto the grid quickly, while keeping costs fair for families. On June 18, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Chairman Laura Swett directed six regional grid operators to justify or update their rules for how data centers and other large loads connect. Swett framed the action around “fair cost allocation, unprecedented transparency for the American ratepayer and speed to power.” Former FERC Chairman Neil Chatterjee explained that the order creates a better regulatory environment for data centers: “[The order] sent a very clear signal that large load interconnections need to be treated differently from typical retail loads, that I think had a huge impact on investors, and just folks that are tracking this space.” Chatterjee added that by leaving grid operators to address the changes they need to speed up interconnections in their own regions; the resulting impact will be: “Faster and more legally durable than a nation-wide rule.” Keeping bills low as demand climbs comes down to one thing: new supply has to keep pace. That’s where natural gas shines. Gas already generates about 41 percent of U.S. electricity, the single largest source on the grid, and it is dispatchable, reliable and affordable, making it the natural choice to power the AI boom. As Energy in Depth has previously analyzed , a recent International Energy Agency study found that for the United States to be able to host a majority (75 percent) of AI computing domestically, it will need to make around 51 gigawatts of electricity available to data centers by 2027. Natural gas, sourced from Appalachia, the Permian and Haynesville regions, can scale quickly and affordably to keep durable new supply flowing to the grid as data centers grow. Bottom line: Data centers have been bringing down household energy costs because of their ability to serve as anchor customers and their investments to help modernize the grid. At the same time, affordable natural gas is the engine keeping that progress going. EPRI’s data underscores that the United States can power the AI boom while protecting ratepayers at the same time.

story.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

facts.text: Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too.
The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 .
And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants .
But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.
Goldman Sachs forecasts a sharp rise in US data-centre capacity, with an additional 52 GW expected by 2028, driven by growing AI infrastructure demand.
This expansion could increase electricity consumption, tighten power markets and boost natural gas prices.
However, tighter regulations following midterm election results may moderate future data-centre development.

extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.” These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores. New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

extraction.body: The AI boom is spawning a wave of data center construction demand in the UK, but insufficient grid connection capacity is forcing some developers to change their energy plans. National Gas, the operator of the UK's gas transmission network, disclosed that large data center projects inquiring with the company about gas connection options have risen to 24 from 5 last year. The direct driver of this shift is excessively long grid connection queues. A combination of factors—planning approvals, regulatory procedures, construction costs and skilled-labor shortages—means some projects must wait years from application to actual connection to the UK's national electricity system. Under these circumstances, some developers are beginning to consider building their own gas-fired generation facilities to meet power needs during the initial phase of project operation. The Quest Park data center campus in Bedfordshire is a typical case. The project has a planned power demand of 720 megawatts and is expected to become one of the UK's largest data center campuses, but constrained by local grid capacity, it is not expected to formally connect to the power system until 2034 at the earliest. A high-pressure gas pipeline happens to pass near the campus, and connection could come significantly earlier, so the developer plans to build a gas-fired power plant first to supply power at least for the project's relatively smaller initial phase. Such considerations are not isolated. The £3 billion (approximately $4.0 billion) SDC M40 Campus in Buckinghamshire, as well as a proposed data center project by Curtis Hall in Cardiff, are both evaluating gas-fired generation as a transitional solution until formal grid connection permits are obtained, according to planning documents. Alan Fotheringham, director of low-carbon global market solutions at consultancy Jacobs, noted that the path to gas-fired generation is much shorter than the path to securing permanent grid connection capacity. The potential incremental demand for gas should not be underestimated. Marten Ford, an analyst at energy research firm Aurora Energy Research, estimates that if data center construction accelerates and renewable energy growth fails to outpace existing plans, UK gas-fired generation could increase by 40 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 44% of the country's gas-fired generation last year. He also emphasized that without broader countermeasures, large-scale deployment of data centers will drive up natural gas use and thereby increase carbon emissions. The above estimates already assume that most proposed projects are speculative investments that will ultimately not materialize. If all these projects were built, the increase in gas demand would be even more significant. Tom Edwards, an analyst at market analysis firm Cornwall Insight, also noted that regardless of the scale of construction, existing gas-fired power plants will need to run more frequently; even if data centers successfully connect to the national grid, the electricity they use comes from a mix of renewables, nuclear and natural gas, which would likewise drive gas demand to some extent. Faced with enormous demand, the UK government has begun adjusting policy. A proposal introduced last week suggests that data centers of strategic importance may be paired with gas-fired generation, provided investors commit that the long-term goal remains connection to the national grid. The proposal is accompanied by a new "commitment agreement" mechanism for data centers, under which paired power plants would not need to undergo separate carbon emissions assessments, with the relevant emissions impact handled by the government at the national level. Within the UK energy industry, there is disagreement over what energy source data centers should use. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy, the UK's largest oil, gas and electricity retailer, disagrees with the view that only natural gas and nuclear power can meet data centers' need for stable electricity supply. He proposes locating more data centers in Scotland to take advantage of the region's abundant wind resources. But real-world constraints are also evident. Many operators want to be close to customer-concentrated areas such as London, while the UK's current electricity market mechanisms lack sufficient incentives for developers to relocate projects to regions richer in renewable energy resources. Wind and solar power face land-use requirements and intermittency issues, energy storage systems are relatively costly, and small modular nuclear reactors remain some distance from large-scale commercial deployment. By contrast, the UK's existing gas pipeline network has broad coverage, and some projects can obtain gas supply more quickly. Real estate consultancy Savills said the market is currently studying multiple energy configuration options, but for some projects that need stable power supply quickly in the near term, natural gas still holds practical appeal. On the environmental front, Natascha Hospedales, head of AI affairs at ClientEarth, criticized the UK government's proposal as amounting to "tacitly allowing data centers to begin construction without simultaneously imposing equally strict environmental constraints." Katie Berriman-Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at tech industry group Tech UK, said that for most developers, the current priority remains advancing reform of the grid connection mechanism and improving related policies so projects can connect faster. In her view, gas-fired generation is more of a realistic transitional measure against the backdrop of long-term grid capacity constraints, rather than a direction of proactive industry transformation. A key variable is the actual scale of projects that materialize. Consultancies estimate that of the data center projects currently queued for grid connection, totaling 73 gigawatts of installed capacity, only 10% to 20% will ultimately be built. UK authorities are trying to accelerate reform of the connection queue while weeding out speculative projects that have no substantive plans to materialize. The practices of other European countries offer a reference. Ford mentioned that Ireland has introduced regulations requiring 80% of data centers' electricity to come from renewable sources, which could serve as a reference model for promoting greater use of clean energy in data centers. For the market, this trend means UK gas demand could gain a new source of growth beyond the power system, and utilization of gas-fired generation and pipeline assets may rise accordingly; but at the same time, the pace at which data center projects materialize, the progress of grid connection reform and the specific implementation standards of the government's "commitment agreements" will all directly affect the actual scale of incremental gas demand. For data center developers, whether they can strike a balance between power supply and emissions-reduction commitments is becoming a key variable in whether projects can be commissioned on schedule. extraction.body: The oil and gas infrastructure company’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them. “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.” In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment. In July, the EPA announced new federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance. That month, the EPA said that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply. Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program. In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter. Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts. Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah. Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added. Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each. Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low. Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says. “If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says. Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says. Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

Hall wrote that the company believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.” The EPA said in its July announcement that the new guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers.
However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection.
These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.
Williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers.
As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country.
Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year.

In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.” “EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.
Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta.

But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed company that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the company’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs.

In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements.

He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.” The Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain.
The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.
Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants.

The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year.
Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants.
But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants.
In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating new regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says.

Both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law.

The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.) When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid.
“No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating.
The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

Some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world.

Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

extraction.body: The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom. One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy. When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them. Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation. Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says. Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says. The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.) Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives. Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources. BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report . That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands. And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices. There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data. Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky. While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.” These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores. New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid. Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.
