extraction.body: The AI boom is spawning a wave of data center construction demand in the UK, but insufficient grid connection capacity is forcing some developers to change their energy plans. National Gas, the operator of the UK's gas transmission network, disclosed that large data center projects inquiring with the company about gas connection options have risen to 24 from 5 last year. The direct driver of this shift is excessively long grid connection queues. A combination of factors—planning approvals, regulatory procedures, construction costs and skilled-labor shortages—means some projects must wait years from application to actual connection to the UK's national electricity system. Under these circumstances, some developers are beginning to consider building their own gas-fired generation facilities to meet power needs during the initial phase of project operation. The Quest Park data center campus in Bedfordshire is a typical case. The project has a planned power demand of 720 megawatts and is expected to become one of the UK's largest data center campuses, but constrained by local grid capacity, it is not expected to formally connect to the power system until 2034 at the earliest. A high-pressure gas pipeline happens to pass near the campus, and connection could come significantly earlier, so the developer plans to build a gas-fired power plant first to supply power at least for the project's relatively smaller initial phase. Such considerations are not isolated. The £3 billion (approximately $4.0 billion) SDC M40 Campus in Buckinghamshire, as well as a proposed data center project by Curtis Hall in Cardiff, are both evaluating gas-fired generation as a transitional solution until formal grid connection permits are obtained, according to planning documents. Alan Fotheringham, director of low-carbon global market solutions at consultancy Jacobs, noted that the path to gas-fired generation is much shorter than the path to securing permanent grid connection capacity. The potential incremental demand for gas should not be underestimated. Marten Ford, an analyst at energy research firm Aurora Energy Research, estimates that if data center construction accelerates and renewable energy growth fails to outpace existing plans, UK gas-fired generation could increase by 40 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 44% of the country's gas-fired generation last year. He also emphasized that without broader countermeasures, large-scale deployment of data centers will drive up natural gas use and thereby increase carbon emissions. The above estimates already assume that most proposed projects are speculative investments that will ultimately not materialize. If all these projects were built, the increase in gas demand would be even more significant. Tom Edwards, an analyst at market analysis firm Cornwall Insight, also noted that regardless of the scale of construction, existing gas-fired power plants will need to run more frequently; even if data centers successfully connect to the national grid, the electricity they use comes from a mix of renewables, nuclear and natural gas, which would likewise drive gas demand to some extent. Faced with enormous demand, the UK government has begun adjusting policy. A proposal introduced last week suggests that data centers of strategic importance may be paired with gas-fired generation, provided investors commit that the long-term goal remains connection to the national grid. The proposal is accompanied by a new "commitment agreement" mechanism for data centers, under which paired power plants would not need to undergo separate carbon emissions assessments, with the relevant emissions impact handled by the government at the national level. Within the UK energy industry, there is disagreement over what energy source data centers should use. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy, the UK's largest oil, gas and electricity retailer, disagrees with the view that only natural gas and nuclear power can meet data centers' need for stable electricity supply. He proposes locating more data centers in Scotland to take advantage of the region's abundant wind resources. But real-world constraints are also evident. Many operators want to be close to customer-concentrated areas such as London, while the UK's current electricity market mechanisms lack sufficient incentives for developers to relocate projects to regions richer in renewable energy resources. Wind and solar power face land-use requirements and intermittency issues, energy storage systems are relatively costly, and small modular nuclear reactors remain some distance from large-scale commercial deployment. By contrast, the UK's existing gas pipeline network has broad coverage, and some projects can obtain gas supply more quickly. Real estate consultancy Savills said the market is currently studying multiple energy configuration options, but for some projects that need stable power supply quickly in the near term, natural gas still holds practical appeal. On the environmental front, Natascha Hospedales, head of AI affairs at ClientEarth, criticized the UK government's proposal as amounting to "tacitly allowing data centers to begin construction without simultaneously imposing equally strict environmental constraints." Katie Berriman-Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at tech industry group Tech UK, said that for most developers, the current priority remains advancing reform of the grid connection mechanism and improving related policies so projects can connect faster. In her view, gas-fired generation is more of a realistic transitional measure against the backdrop of long-term grid capacity constraints, rather than a direction of proactive industry transformation. A key variable is the actual scale of projects that materialize. Consultancies estimate that of the data center projects currently queued for grid connection, totaling 73 gigawatts of installed capacity, only 10% to 20% will ultimately be built. UK authorities are trying to accelerate reform of the connection queue while weeding out speculative projects that have no substantive plans to materialize. The practices of other European countries offer a reference. Ford mentioned that Ireland has introduced regulations requiring 80% of data centers' electricity to come from renewable sources, which could serve as a reference model for promoting greater use of clean energy in data centers. For the market, this trend means UK gas demand could gain a new source of growth beyond the power system, and utilization of gas-fired generation and pipeline assets may rise accordingly; but at the same time, the pace at which data center projects materialize, the progress of grid connection reform and the specific implementation standards of the government's "commitment agreements" will all directly affect the actual scale of incremental gas demand. For data center developers, whether they can strike a balance between power supply and emissions-reduction commitments is becoming a key variable in whether projects can be commissioned on schedule. passages: The AI boom is spawning a wave of data center construction demand in the UK, but insufficient grid connection capacity is forcing some developers to change their energy plans. National Gas, the operator of the UK's gas transmission network, disclosed that large data center projects inquiring with the company about gas connection options have risen to 24 from 5 last year.

The direct driver of this shift is excessively long grid connection queues. A combination of factors—planning approvals, regulatory procedures, construction costs and skilled-labor shortages—means some projects must wait years from application to actual connection to the UK's national electricity system. Under these circumstances, some developers are beginning to consider building their own gas-fired generation facilities to meet power needs during the initial phase of project operation.

The Quest Park data center campus in Bedfordshire is a typical case. The project has a planned power demand of 720 megawatts and is expected to become one of the UK's largest data center campuses, but constrained by local grid capacity, it is not expected to formally connect to the power system until 2034 at the earliest. A high-pressure gas pipeline happens to pass near the campus, and connection could come significantly earlier, so the developer plans to build a gas-fired power plant first to supply power at least for the project's relatively smaller initial phase.

Such considerations are not isolated. The £3 billion (approximately $4.0 billion) SDC M40 Campus in Buckinghamshire, as well as a proposed data center project by Curtis Hall in Cardiff, are both evaluating gas-fired generation as a transitional solution until formal grid connection permits are obtained, according to planning documents. Alan Fotheringham, director of low-carbon global market solutions at consultancy Jacobs, noted that the path to gas-fired generation is much shorter than the path to securing permanent grid connection capacity.

The potential incremental demand for gas should not be underestimated. Marten Ford, an analyst at energy research firm Aurora Energy Research, estimates that if data center construction accelerates and renewable energy growth fails to outpace existing plans, UK gas-fired generation could increase by 40 terawatt-hours by 2035, equivalent to 44% of the country's gas-fired generation last year. He also emphasized that without broader countermeasures, large-scale deployment of data centers will drive up natural gas use and thereby increase carbon emissions.

The above estimates already assume that most proposed projects are speculative investments that will ultimately not materialize. If all these projects were built, the increase in gas demand would be even more significant. Tom Edwards, an analyst at market analysis firm Cornwall Insight, also noted that regardless of the scale of construction, existing gas-fired power plants will need to run more frequently; even if data centers successfully connect to the national grid, the electricity they use comes from a mix of renewables, nuclear and natural gas, which would likewise drive gas demand to some extent.

Faced with enormous demand, the UK government has begun adjusting policy. A proposal introduced last week suggests that data centers of strategic importance may be paired with gas-fired generation, provided investors commit that the long-term goal remains connection to the national grid. The proposal is accompanied by a new "commitment agreement" mechanism for data centers, under which paired power plants would not need to undergo separate carbon emissions assessments, with the relevant emissions impact handled by the government at the national level.

Within the UK energy industry, there is disagreement over what energy source data centers should use. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy, the UK's largest oil, gas and electricity retailer, disagrees with the view that only natural gas and nuclear power can meet data centers' need for stable electricity supply. He proposes locating more data centers in Scotland to take advantage of the region's abundant wind resources.

But real-world constraints are also evident. Many operators want to be close to customer-concentrated areas such as London, while the UK's current electricity market mechanisms lack sufficient incentives for developers to relocate projects to regions richer in renewable energy resources. Wind and solar power face land-use requirements and intermittency issues, energy storage systems are relatively costly, and small modular nuclear reactors remain some distance from large-scale commercial deployment. By contrast, the UK's existing gas pipeline network has broad coverage, and some projects can obtain gas supply more quickly. Real estate consultancy Savills said the market is currently studying multiple energy configuration options, but for some projects that need stable power supply quickly in the near term, natural gas still holds practical appeal.

On the environmental front, Natascha Hospedales, head of AI affairs at ClientEarth, criticized the UK government's proposal as amounting to "tacitly allowing data centers to begin construction without simultaneously imposing equally strict environmental constraints."

Katie Berriman-Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at tech industry group Tech UK, said that for most developers, the current priority remains advancing reform of the grid connection mechanism and improving related policies so projects can connect faster. In her view, gas-fired generation is more of a realistic transitional measure against the backdrop of long-term grid capacity constraints, rather than a direction of proactive industry transformation.

A key variable is the actual scale of projects that materialize. Consultancies estimate that of the data center projects currently queued for grid connection, totaling 73 gigawatts of installed capacity, only 10% to 20% will ultimately be built. UK authorities are trying to accelerate reform of the connection queue while weeding out speculative projects that have no substantive plans to materialize.

The practices of other European countries offer a reference. Ford mentioned that Ireland has introduced regulations requiring 80% of data centers' electricity to come from renewable sources, which could serve as a reference model for promoting greater use of clean energy in data centers.

For the market, this trend means UK gas demand could gain a new source of growth beyond the power system, and utilization of gas-fired generation and pipeline assets may rise accordingly; but at the same time, the pace at which data center projects materialize, the progress of grid connection reform and the specific implementation standards of the government's "commitment agreements" will all directly affect the actual scale of incremental gas demand. For data center developers, whether they can strike a balance between power supply and emissions-reduction commitments is becoming a key variable in whether projects can be commissioned on schedule.

However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection.

Williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta.
Natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants.
BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US.

passages: 1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems.
The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident.
The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.
It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts.
The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks.
Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data.

The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers. It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess. The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

passages: “On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” the company detailed.

The records pulled down by the malicious code belong to “a subset of our users,” and 1Password hasn’t said how many people that covers or whether individual, business or family accounts were affected.
Each record holds the name and email address a customer uses with 1Password, account and user identifiers, the date the account was created and the time of its last sign-in.
The attacker also got the public keys tied to those accounts, which are “public by design” and have “no impact to user security,” the company noted.
Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters were taken too, and 1Password maintains these “cannot be used to access your account.”
Internal credentials that may have leaked were rotated or revoked.
No action is needed on customers’ accounts, 1Password advised.

“We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password,” the post reads , and the warning extends to texts and phone calls that mention invitations or account recovery.
On top of that, 1Password said it has tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, added new detections, and brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate the cleanup.
“1Password identified a security incident involving some of our backend systems,” the company wrote in a post it plans to keep updated.
“Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets,” 1Password noted.
“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated.
Tokens from invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails were copied, though a token only works “when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code.”

extraction.body: Password manager 1Password has suffered a backend breach after an attacker took over a staff member's corporate GitHub account and used it to take customer account data. The company began investigating on November 19 after detecting signs of the intrusion, it said in an incident post . "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password wrote. With the GitHub account, the attacker reached 1Password's source code and pushed malicious code into backend services, which then pulled administrative records on a subset of users. Private repository code was also copied, and the attacker got into the company's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) system. 1Password said the source code held no user secrets, but the CI/CD environment contained infrastructure secrets, which it rotated. Exposed records included customers' names, email addresses, account and user IDs, the dates accounts were created and last signed in, public keys and parameters used by the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol. Tokens in some invitation, provisioning and recovery emails were also exposed, and those affected, "a small number of users," were told directly. 1Password said a token only worked together with a single sign-on (SSO) login or a code emailed to the account's address. The keys protecting vaults, account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and its browser extensions were not affected, the company said. It added that it did not store users' account passwords or Secret Keys. 1Password shut down the compromised GitHub account, canceled the token the attacker had stolen and cut off their access. It also rotated or revoked internal credentials that might have been exposed, tightened controls around GitHub, CI/CD and endpoints and introduced new detections. As a precaution, 1Password lengthened invitation and recovery codes to 10 letters and numbers, up from six digits. It also engaged outside security experts to verify its containment and clean-up work. The company said customers did not need to change anything in their accounts but should watch for phishing, such as unexpected invitations or recovery requests. Its internal checks found no evidence that exposed provisioning tokens had been used to take over accounts, and the company said it would update its post if anything changed.

story.title: 1Password breached through hijacked employee GitHub account, customer names and emails stolen - Help Net Security

facts.text: 1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems.
The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident.
The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.
It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts.
The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks.
Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data.
“On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers,” the company detailed.
Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here!

The records pulled down by the malicious code belong to “a subset of our users,” and 1Password hasn’t said how many people that covers or whether individual, business or family accounts were affected.
Each record holds the name and email address a customer uses with 1Password, account and user identifiers, the date the account was created and the time of its last sign-in.
The attacker also got the public keys tied to those accounts, which are “public by design” and have “no impact to user security,” the company noted.
Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol parameters were taken too, and 1Password maintains these “cannot be used to access your account.”
Internal credentials that may have leaked were rotated or revoked.
No action is needed on customers’ accounts, 1Password advised.

“We recommend being cautious of phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails about 1Password,” the post reads , and the warning extends to texts and phone calls that mention invitations or account recovery.
On top of that, 1Password said it has tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, added new detections, and brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate the cleanup.
“1Password identified a security incident involving some of our backend systems,” the company wrote in a post it plans to keep updated.
“Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets,” 1Password noted.
“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” 1Password stated.
Tokens from invitation, provisioning and account recovery emails were copied, though a token only works “when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code.”

Black Friday might still be a few days away, but some great smart glasses deals are already slipping through. There are plenty of great options to choose from, which will likely suit the needs of different users. Whether you’re looking to put a massive virtual screen in front of your eyes, record videos without reaching for your phone, or experiment with wearable AI, you have something for everyone. And the savings aren’t bad, either. XREAL is knocking $100 off its One Pro glasses, VITURE has discounted its Luma Ultra by $150, and Meta is offering 25% off selected Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses. So I’ve narrowed things down to six deals worth checking out, covering everything from gaming and portable entertainment to hands-free photography and AI assistance. XREAL has a great deal for you if you’re looking to turn any compatible device into a massive personal screen. The XREAL One Pro is a great deal, which basically turns it into a wearable display that lets you enjoy movies, games, and even desktop applications without needing a physical monitor in front of you. At $499, down from $599, the One Pro is worth considering if you’ve been waiting to try a high-end wearable display. INAIR Pod is an ideal companion for compatible AR glasses, bringing Android apps and spatial computing to selected models from VITURE, XREAL, and RayNeo. Run supported apps directly on the Pod and create a workspace with up to six virtual windows in supported INAIR configurations. Spatial features and window availability vary by glasses model. Get it for $351.99, down from $439.99 . For an integrated setup, the INAIR 2 Go Pack puts a portable spatial workstation in your bag. It combines INAIR 2 Pro glasses, INAIR Pod, a foldable keyboard, and a carrying case for work and entertainment on the go—from browsing and writing to watching your favorite content. Get the bundle for $799.20, down from $999 . Ray-Ban Meta glasses are still one of the easiest ways to try smart eyewear without committing to something that looks a little too futuristic. The second-generation models retain Ray-Ban’s familiar styling while adding an upgraded camera, improved battery life, and Meta AI integration. You get a 12MP camera capable of recording video at up to 3K resolution, along with open-ear speakers and microphones for music, phone calls, and voice commands. Meta AI can also help answer questions about your surroundings, provide information, and assist with supported translation features. Battery life is rated for up to eight hours of typical use, with the included charging case providing additional power throughout the day. Meta’s Black Friday promotion takes 25% off eligible Gen 2 models, bringing the starting price down from $379 to $284.25. The VITURE Luma Ultra is another excellent option for anyone who wants a private virtual display, which is great if gaming and watching movies are high on the priority list. The VITURE Luma Ultra is another excellent option for anyone who wants a private virtual display, particularly if gaming and watching movies are high on the priority list. The glasses also support spatial features, including six-degrees-of-freedom tracking and hand gestures when used with compatible software and accessories. VITURE’s Black Friday sale brings the Luma Ultra down to $449 from $599. Want a more sporty look with the Meta smart glasses tech? Well, you can check out the Oakley Meta HSTN. It combines Oakley’s distinctive eyewear design with the camera, audio, and AI capabilities of Meta’s smart glasses platform. The HSTN features a 12MP camera with 3K video recording, open-ear speakers, and built-in microphones. This makes it great for capturing hands-free footage during walks, outdoor adventures, and other activities where pulling out a smartphone isn’t convenient. There’s also an IPX4 water-resistance rating, providing protection against splashes, sweat, and light rain. Meta advertises up to eight hours of battery life under typical usage conditions, with additional charging available through the included case. With a 25% Black Friday discount, the starting price falls to $299.30, down from $399. It’s a handy alternative to the Ray-Ban models for buyers who prefer Oakley’s styling and sport-oriented lenses. The RayNeo Air 4 Pro is one of the more affordable ways to get a large virtual screen for gaming and entertainment. One of its standout features is HDR10 support, designed to deliver better highlight and shadow detail when viewing compatible content. The glasses use Micro-OLED displays with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. So they are comfortable for gaming. You also get RayNeo’s Vision 4000 processing chip, which supports features such as SDR-to-HDR conversion, along with audio tuned by Bang & Olufsen. There’s compatibility with supported USB-C devices, including smartphones, laptops, and handheld gaming systems. As with most wearable displays, the connected device must support the appropriate video output, or you may need an additional adapter. At a current advertised price of $233.22, down from $299, the Air 4 Pro is one of the least expensive display-equipped glasses in this roundup. The Rokid AI Glasses Style is a little different from the wearable displays in this roundup. Rather than putting a screen in front of your eyes, they’re designed around everyday AI assistance, audio, and hands-free photography. At just 38.5 grams without prescription lenses, they’re also relatively lightweight. Rokid has equipped them with a 12MP Sony camera capable of recording up to 3K video, along with open-ear audio and voice-based AI assistance. The glasses can help with supported tasks such as translation, answering questions, and capturing photos or videos from your perspective. They connect to a smartphone through the Hi Rokid app, which also manages supported features and settings. Rokid’s Black Friday deal lists the AI Glasses Style for $279, down from a $399 comparison price. It’s a good choice if you want to try out an AI assistant and camera built into ordinary-looking eyewear rather than watching movies on a virtual screen. I've tried a bunch of open-ear earbuds over the last couple of years. While I don't personally gravitate towards them, they serve a few specific and useful features. The freedom they offer has its perks, but they aren't always comfortable--at least for me. While you can regularly find decent markdowns on TVs from pretty much every brand throughout the year, Cyber Week sales are still a great opportunity to upgrade your screen or pick up a second TV for your bedroom. You’ll also have an easier time finding discounted TV and soundbar bundles for a complete home theater upgrade on the cheap.

Since November is packed with savings across retailers, there are plenty of opportunities to snag deals on top TVs. Cyber Week is usually when you can find the most substantial discounts, but with many sales starting earlier and earlier, the week before Thanksgiving is another popular time for brands to kick off deals. At the very least, you can find great deals from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday.

The best TV to purchase is the one that fits your space and your needs. This varies for everyone, but if you’re searching for specific features or sizes, make sure to use filter options when deal hunting this holiday season. Generally, 55-inch, 65-inch, and 75-inch are fairly common TV sizes for main living areas, but there are larger screen options for home theaters, and smaller ones for bedrooms or other areas of your home.
Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals are relatively comparable, often offering substantial savings on a wide array of items. However, Cyber Monday deals are usually available more online.

extraction.body: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board? Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world. Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology. From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes. In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist. That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one. It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC. That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ. "The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports". Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island. To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors. On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain. Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics. "Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says. In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025. In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States. For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC. In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation. In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story. Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open." However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better. Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China. Jensen Huang signs a Taiwanese banknote for a visitor at Computex 2026 in Taipei This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment. Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang. Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks. "Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank. Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets. Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat. Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry. "I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said. Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world. Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology. From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes. In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist. That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one. It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC. That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ. "The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports". Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island. To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors. On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain. Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics. "Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says. In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025. In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States. For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC. In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation. In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story. Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open." However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better. Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China. Jensen Huang signs a Taiwanese banknote for a visitor at Computex 2026 in Taipei This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment. Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang. Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks. "Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank. Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets. Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat. Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry. "I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said. extraction.body: CNBC reported on November 26, 2026 that Nvidia chip sellers have told neocloud operators, which rent out accelerated computing capacity, they will not supply GPUs if any of the resulting computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, citing two people familiar with the private communications. The condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds. The disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases. The seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS said the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments. The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations. Aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case. Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end users that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries. The reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. sources.title: Nvidia sellers seek buyers after US restrictions on China — CNBC - UA.NEWS
passages: In the United States, sellers of Nvidia graphics processing units are seeking new buyers after rules were tightened restricting remote access by China-linked companies to advanced computing power for artificial intelligence.
CNBC reports that an unusually large volume of offers to sell Nvidia GPUs appeared on the market after the new measures were announced.
According to three CNBC sources, the increase in the number of GPUs put up for sale is directly linked to the new rule.
These restrictions effectively prohibit the direct sale to China of Nvidia's most advanced chips, but Chinese companies could access them remotely through data centers abroad.
Nvidia declined to comment, while the Bureau of Industry and Security did not respond to CNBC's request.
During a third-quarter earnings call on November 17, Nvidia's then acting CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the new restrictions.
At the same time, she expected Nvidia's performance to remain strong, as demand for chips significantly exceeds supply.

The condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds. The disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases. The seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS said the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments. The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations. Aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case. Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end users that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries. The reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Under the reported condition, a neocloud’s hardware access depends on the customers its capacity will serve, wherever the data center is located. At the same time, she expected Nvidia's performance to remain strong, as demand for chips significantly exceeds supply.

facts.text: Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter.
Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.
The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.

Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov.
The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power.
Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.

Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes." Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.

The condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had said it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity.

Every GPU that powers a model training cluster has to be built somewhere, and that somewhere is almost always a fab operated by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM). Taiwan Semi does not design the artificial intelligence (AI) chips that get the headlines. Instead, the company manufactures them at nodes no one else can reliably hit at scale. That quiet competitive advantage has turned TSMC into the physical backbone of the AI infrastructure buildout. Nevertheless, the conversation still seems to start and end with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD), or Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). Continue » This gap is strange once you understand how the AI chip stack works. While designers continue to fight over architecture and software, the constraint that decides how many of those designs actually ship is advanced-node capacity -- and TSMC owns most of that market. Nvidia and AMD design GPUs while Micron builds memory solutions layered alongside these chips. None of these companies do all of the manufacturing work to bring their products to life, however. TSMC holds roughly 73% of the pure-play foundry market as measured by revenue and reportedly closer to 90% of the market for the most advanced nodes. For years, Apple was credited as TSMC's largest customer. However, Nvidia took over that title earlier this year. This shift directly tracks the AI infrastructure cycle. High-performance computing, the area that covers AI accelerators and related server silicon, has become Taiwan Semi's core growth engine. The company's management points to AI-accelerator revenue compounding in the mid-to-high 50% range through the end of the decade, and lifted its longer-term company revenue growth outlook toward at least 25%. While competition from Samsung and Intel exist, both companies are spending heavily on scaling foundry operations and neither company is yet to close the gap on the yield and volume at nodes Nvidia and AMD actually need for current and next-generation accelerators. TSMC's financial growth supports the idea that the AI infrastructure supercycle is more than a temporary surge. Full-year 2025 revenue reached about $122 billion, up nearly 36% year over year. Meanwhile, gross margin climbed to 60% from 56% percent the year before. Through the first half of 2026, Taiwan Semi's revenue grew 37% year over year to $76.1 billion while while gross margin expanded into the mid-60% range, underscoring the level of pricing power the company commands right now. The company is also spending heavily on capital expenditures (capex) to help stay ahead of demand. Rising infrastructure spend might look expensive in any single year, but over a multi-year AI buildout it is what keeps the company's moat intact. Customers cannot easily dual-source manufacturing for leading edge nodes. This makes Taiwan Semi's revenue and profit tailwinds tied to the duration of the infrastructure supercycle itself rather than to one specific product launch. The chart below illustrates how investors are treating TSMC as a picks-and-shovels name that should trade at a discount to some of the primary chip designers. Trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) puts the stock near 34 times, which looks rich upon first glance. But on a forward P/E basis, Taiwan Semi is a different story. While the company's forward P/E of 28 is not a deep-value multiple per se, it is also not stretched against a company still expected to grow revenue by a high double-digit percent range and compound earnings as margins hold. Nvidia and AMD capture more of the narrative premium because their products are visible. For the time being, Micron will ride the memory upcycle that AI also requires. Taiwan Semi sits underneath all of them. While geopolitical risk around Taiwan is an obvious factor to consider, in addition to the cost of building fabs here in the U.S., they do not erase a foundry position that remains the hardest part of the AI supply chain to replicate. On a forward earnings valuation basis, I think TSMC stock still looks like a strong candidate to buy and hold throughout the AI infrastructure era. Taiwan Semi's latest earnings report displayed how its business is becoming more valuable than ever to the AI infrastructure era. Nvidia is the undisputed king in the AI accelerator market thanks to its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking technology, and CUDA software ecosystem. However, the company's largest customers are developing alternatives. Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta Platforms are investing in application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) optimized for their own AI workloads. While these chips won't replace Nvidia's GPUs entirely, they should reduce dependence on Nvidia while giving the hyperscalers more control over infrastructure costs and model performance. Meanwhile, Nvidia is also exploring agentic AI , autonomous vehicles, and robotics. Indeed, these opportunities could be enormous. But commercial adoption may take longer than the next four years. Micron is looking at a different challenge. The company's memory solutions are essential for AI computing, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM. Memory manufacturing has historically been a cyclical industry, meaning today's shortages and elevated prices will lead producers to expand capacity. By next decade, more supply should come online, leading to pricing pressure and eroding profit margins. Moreover, competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) also deserves attention. Nevertheless, Advanced Micro Devices is investing aggressively in its Instinct accelerator portfolio, while some of Nvidia's largest customers are developing custom silicon. Broadcom has emerged as an important partner in the market for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), most notably through its relationship with Alphabet and its tensor processing units (TPUs). Meanwhile, Microsoft and Amazon are also developing their own chip portfolios, including Maia, Trainium, and Inferentia. Another potential source of competition is Space Exploration Technologies ' collaboration with Intel on Terafab. Terafab is Elon Musk's semiconductor manufacturing initiative that could eventually reduce SpaceX's dependence on third-party chip suppliers. Although commercial-scale production remains uncertain, the project underscores a growing appetite for vertically integrated semiconductor solutions. Micron faces a different set of challenges. While the proliferation of generative AI has ushered in a memory supercycle, memory-intensive applications such as humanoid robotics and autonomous vehicles should introduce additional tailwinds over the next several years. However, Micron competes against Samsung and SK Hynix in the high bandwidth memory (HBM) market. Furthermore, memory pricing has historically been cyclical, leaving producers vulnerable to fluctuations in supply, demand, and profitability. While Nvidia and Micron could both continue thriving, there is an alternative way to invest in the semiconductor industry without betting on a particular chip designer or memory manufacturer. Unlike Nvidia and AMD, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) primarily manufactures semiconductors designed by other companies. Its customer base includes businesses spanning GPUs, custom AI accelerators, smartphone processors, and automotive chips. Against this backdrop, if Nvidia continues to dominate the AI accelerator market, TSMC benefits. Should AMD start to capture additional market share or custom ASICs become increasingly popular, TSMC still stands to benefit because it manufactures chips across these competing architectures as well. Interestingly, Taiwan Semi also has exposure to the memory supercycle. While the company isn't a producer of conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), its collaboration with SK Hynix involves manufacturing logic base dies for next-generation HBM4 solutions. Moreover, TSMC's advanced packaging technologies -- particularly its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) platform -- play a critical role in integrating AI processors with HBM. As a result, growing demand for more sophisticated memory configurations creates additional markets for TSMC beyond traditional wafer fabrication. The most compelling aspect of TSMC's competitive positioning is the sheer magnitude of its market share. Industry estimates suggest that Taiwan Semi controls roughly 73% of the global pure-play foundry market . By contrast, the next closest competitor sits at just 6%. Although TSMC isn't technically a monopoly, its dominance gives it the characteristics of one. The company's manufacturing expertise, technological edge, production scale, and customer relationships are simply too difficult for the competition to replicate at scale. Meanwhile, the company's gross margin reached nearly 65%, and its operating margin expanded to about 59%. Management expects revenue to reach $53.3 billion in the fourth quarter, implying 58% year-over-year growth. That valuation profile looks attractive for a business generating this level of growth and profitability while commanding such a dominant market position. extraction.body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans. While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page. Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September. The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs. extraction.body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage. The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees . Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. passages: ChatGPT users working with GPT-6.2 will now run into their usage limits sooner.
Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced the fix on X on November 26.
From now on, "the same work will use more of your plan's usage allowance." Compared with the previous week, users will reach their limits 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol.
Other models were not affected, and OpenAI will not charge for the difference on past usage.
OpenAI has already announced the next change.
Starting in December, Plus, Pro and Business plans will share one allowance across ChatGPT and Codex, measured in tokens, the units of text a model processes and generates.
The help center says usage "will depend on the model you choose and the task you ask it to do." Instant chat will not draw from the allowance.

OpenAI expects that most users "won't need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do now." According to TechCrunch , a small group of Pro subscribers has been on the shared meter since November 24.
We explained what the merger means for Plus subscribers in early November.
After the switch, Settings and Usage will show how much is left.
Heavy Astra users are better off moving routine work to Sol or Instant.
Our comparison of AI subscriptions shows what OpenAI, Google and Anthropic charge.
A banked reset is a one-time refresh of your allowance that stays saved to your account until you choose to use it.
A reset only works once at least one of the allowances it covers has less than 80% remaining.
On Plus, it restores the five-hour and weekly allowances to 100%, while on Go it restores the monthly allowance.
Each reset has an expiration date that is shown before you confirm it, so it makes sense to save it for a day when you are close to the limit.
Astra and Sol have been available in ChatGPT Work and Codex since November 17.

The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms. The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024. "It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said. Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps. TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data. Startups DramaBox and ReelShort beat out entertainment giants Netflix and Disney in average mobile usage time in the U.S. in the third quarter, according to Sensor Tower. As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in. Fox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas. The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025. Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app. Thus far, hits include dark academia series "Secret Society: Till Blood Do Us Part" and "Kiss of the Pirate King." Individual series have reached tens of millions of views, according to the company. Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience. Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit. "One of the exciting things that we learned when we started talking to studios in Hollywood around two years ago is that all of them are super hungry for consumer data," Nesvit said. "They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content." Nesvit said the company will provide studios with feedback on everything from the length of a camera shot to what color dress a character should wear. "Our goal is how we can drive audiences from YouTube, from TikTok, from Instagram to our platform, and also create those kinds of synergies [with] legacy media," he said. Holywater recently adapted Season 3 of Fox's reality TV hit "Farmer Wants a Wife" into a microseries fit for the platform. The company also plans to create a scripted series featuring 30 three-minute episodes inspired by Fox's "Fear Factor: House of Fear." Holywater currently relies on a combination of subscription fees, which make up about 80% of its revenue, and money from advertisers. Nesvit said the company is also exploring incorporating brand integrations. The company is already profitable, its co-founders said. "You attract organically the audience that loves that [intellectual property]," he said. While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house. Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun, who have collectively held leadership roles at NBCUniversal, Showtime, Warner Bros. Discovery and ABC, have jointly founded a microdrama startup called aTwist. "One of the specialties that we have is really what it means to be a great storyteller," Rovner told CNBC in an interview. "I was president of Warner Bros. Television. I was there for 22 years. "But it also gives these linear networks the opportunity to get programming at an incredibly low cost that, from what we're seeing, the audience loves." Large streaming companies, which have already faced competition from social media apps and YouTube, are exploring ways to incorporate microdramas inside their existing apps. NBCUniversal's Peacock launched its own vertical video channel within the app this summer that features both original unscripted series and more traditional vertical dramas . NBCUniversal is also eyeing international development by investing in an Indian microdrama platform , EloElo Group's Story TV, earlier this month. "At NBCUniversal, we see significant opportunity in mobile-first storytelling and emerging formats like microdramas to engage audiences and meet evolving viewing habits," Deepak Arya, executive vice president for corporate strategy and development at NBCUniversal, said in a press release . Disney+ , Paramount+ and Netflix similarly launched vertical channels embedded in their services this year. Notably, the channels are meant to help viewers discover traditional content and so far haven't featured original, vertical-first series. Despite the flurry of investment, Hollywood still faces the challenge of how to translate viewing hours into profit, especially for shorter content. Leading U.S. microdrama app ReelShort posted a net loss of $12 million in 2025 despite bringing in total revenue of $785 million, according to research compiled by Media Partners Asia, or MPA. The app, which was founded in 2022 by California-based Crazy Maple Studio, currently reaches about 65 million users every month, according to the company's LinkedIn profile .

Spending on U.S. film productions rose 4% in the most recent quarter, thanks in part to tax incentives, according to research firm ProdPro. But globally it is still down.‘DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE’Microdramas are succeeding because they apply a centuries-old formula — the cliffhanger — to the ubiquitous smart phone that Emarketer estimates accounts for 99 minutes of video viewing each day for the average American. Episodes range from 45 seconds to two minutes long, leaving little time for lengthy plot set-ups.”You’re dropped right into the middle of the story, so it grabs your attention right away,” said Lily Darragh Harty, director of production at Inkitt CandyJar, a platform for romance microdramas.Some 66 million monthly active users watched microdramas last year in the U.S., more than double the 26 million in 2024, according to research firm Omdia. Women aged 25 to 55 make up the core user base.The little-known studios behind the phenomenon are raking in dollars. CandyJar, a two year-old platform that releases a new romance about once a week, is on track to generate more than $100 million in annual sales. According to its executives, each microdrama series typically spans 50 to 75 episodes, and takes about three months to produce at a cost of between $100,000 to $300,000. A typical half-hour sitcom costs between $2 million and $4 million per episode.CandyJar’s ”romance-forward” platform attracts a 99.9% female audience, said Elana Zeltser, director of creative development for Inkitt CandyJar. Males account for 30% of the users on MyDrama, according to a new poll by Owl & Co. Veteran media executives have gotten into the act, including former Miramax CEO Bill Block, who launched a vertical drama app called GammaTime, and former ABC Entertainment Chairman Lloyd Braun, who is backing a studio and platform called aTwist.ATwist co-founders Jana Winograde, the former president of Showtime, and Susan Rovner, a veteran of NBCUniversal and Warner Bros. Television, said they’re using everything they learned about how to quickly hook a television audience. They plan to deliver 20 to 30 microseries, spanning various genres, including romance, thrillers and unscripted content, in the coming months.“We’re not looking to win Emmys, we’re looking to win the People’s Choice Awards,” said Rovner.‘MAKE THIS CHARACTER SMILE’As the broader Hollywood community contends with the benefits and perils of AI, microdramas have embraced the technology.To attract a male audience, CandyJar’s sister platform Ironblood has started churning out action-focused microdramas made even more quickly and cheaply — using generative artificial intelligence. A human director uses prompts to direct the story.“I can make any change in two minutes,” said Inkitt Ironblood producer and editor Elizabeth Knebel, who incorporates revisions requested by directors.“If they want the character to smile, I can go into the prompt, say ‘make this character smile,’ and it’s done immediately,” she said.San Francisco-based Inkitt has about 135 employees and has hired 35 of them in recent weeks, said CEO Ali Albazaz. The company is adding one or two new video producers each week to ramp up productions for what Albazaz sees as “the renaissance of Hollywood.”The new format has come with new rules and standards. SAG-AFTRA, the union that represents actors, stunt performers and others, created a new media contract that sets minimum pay rates, mandated rest periods and safety rules.Not long ago, Hollywood hopefuls followed a well-worn path to discovery. A commercial gig followed by work as an extra, then getting an agent before booking that sitcom, and then, for the lucky few, a successful career. But that arc has changed, according to Hernan Lopez, the head of Owl, who was previously president and CEO of Fox International.“Today, you hear anecdotally of many people coming to L.A. and getting their first job through a vertical drama.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience.
Fox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas.
The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025.
Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app.
The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data.
NBCUniversal's Peacock launched its own vertical video channel within the app this summer that features both original unscripted series and more traditional vertical dramas .
Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year.
As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in.
During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest."
Despite the flurry of investment, Hollywood still faces the challenge of how to translate viewing hours into profit, especially for shorter content.
"They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content."
While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house.
Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit.
