extraction.body: Bogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century." Nesvit is the co-founder of microseries app My Drama, built around the latest, bite-sized form of storytelling. Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year. They often feature romantic tropes and typically end in cliffhangers to keep viewers hooked. The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms. The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024. "It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said. Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps. TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data. Startups DramaBox and ReelShort beat out entertainment giants Netflix and Disney in average mobile usage time in the U.S. in the third quarter, according to Sensor Tower. As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in. Fox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas. The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025. Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app. Thus far, hits include dark academia series "Secret Society: Till Blood Do Us Part" and "Kiss of the Pirate King." Individual series have reached tens of millions of views, according to the company. Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience. Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit. "One of the exciting things that we learned when we started talking to studios in Hollywood around two years ago is that all of them are super hungry for consumer data," Nesvit said. "They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content." Nesvit said the company will provide studios with feedback on everything from the length of a camera shot to what color dress a character should wear. "Our goal is how we can drive audiences from YouTube, from TikTok, from Instagram to our platform, and also create those kinds of synergies [with] legacy media," he said. Holywater recently adapted Season 3 of Fox's reality TV hit "Farmer Wants a Wife" into a microseries fit for the platform. The company also plans to create a scripted series featuring 30 three-minute episodes inspired by Fox's "Fear Factor: House of Fear." Holywater currently relies on a combination of subscription fees, which make up about 80% of its revenue, and money from advertisers. Nesvit said the company is also exploring incorporating brand integrations. The company is already profitable, its co-founders said. "You attract organically the audience that loves that [intellectual property]," he said. While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house. Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun, who have collectively held leadership roles at NBCUniversal, Showtime, Warner Bros. Discovery and ABC, have jointly founded a microdrama startup called aTwist. "One of the specialties that we have is really what it means to be a great storyteller," Rovner told CNBC in an interview. "I was president of Warner Bros. Television. I was there for 22 years. During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest." "A lot of our competitors' completion rates are very low, their churn rates are very high," Rovner said. "They can often bring people into the store but they can't keep them." The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data. The market intelligence firm notes that the number of users lost in each quarter this year has roughly equaled the number of users gained. ATwist seeks to keep viewers enticed through high-stakes, compelling characters and unique stories. The app has already ordered second seasons of shows and puts a particular emphasis on talent, according to the co-founders. Other series that debuted last month included "Honey, I Think Our House Is Haunted" starring Mario Lopez and "Unboxing the Killer Doll" starring Paris Hilton. In May, aTwist announced an exclusive partnership with Skydance's linear television channel BET to create horizontal microdramas that air first on BET and later stream in vertical format on aTwist's app. "That brings a lot of awareness to our brand, a lot of marketing," Winograde said. "But it also gives these linear networks the opportunity to get programming at an incredibly low cost that, from what we're seeing, the audience loves." Large streaming companies, which have already faced competition from social media apps and YouTube, are exploring ways to incorporate microdramas inside their existing apps. NBCUniversal's Peacock launched its own vertical video channel within the app this summer that features both original unscripted series and more traditional vertical dramas . NBCUniversal is also eyeing international development by investing in an Indian microdrama platform , EloElo Group's Story TV, earlier this month. "At NBCUniversal, we see significant opportunity in mobile-first storytelling and emerging formats like microdramas to engage audiences and meet evolving viewing habits," Deepak Arya, executive vice president for corporate strategy and development at NBCUniversal, said in a press release . Disney+ , Paramount+ and Netflix similarly launched vertical channels embedded in their services this year. Notably, the channels are meant to help viewers discover traditional content and so far haven't featured original, vertical-first series. On top of those media companies, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios Mike Hopkins told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in an interview last month that the tech company was interested in producing its own microdramas. Despite the flurry of investment, Hollywood still faces the challenge of how to translate viewing hours into profit, especially for shorter content. Leading U.S. microdrama app ReelShort posted a net loss of $12 million in 2025 despite bringing in total revenue of $785 million, according to research compiled by Media Partners Asia, or MPA. The app, which was founded in 2022 by California-based Crazy Maple Studio, currently reaches about 65 million users every month, according to the company's LinkedIn profile .

extraction.body: The U.S. microdrama industry is projected to generate $1.5 billion in revenue in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. Fox and NBCUniversal are among the legacy entertainment companies experimenting with vertical videos. High user-acquisition and content costs remain a hurdle even as leading microdrama apps attract large audiences. Bogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century." Nesvit is the co-founder of microseries app My Drama, built around the latest, bite-sized form of storytelling. Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year. The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms. The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024. "It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said. Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps. TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data. As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in. Enter Fox Entertainment Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas. The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025. Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app. Thus far, hits include dark academia series "Secret Society: Till Blood Do Us Part" and "Kiss of the Pirate King." Individual series have reached tens of millions of views, according to the company. Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience. Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit. "One of the exciting things that we learned when we started talking to studios in Hollywood around two years ago is that all of them are super hungry for consumer data," Nesvit said. "They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content." Nesvit said the company will provide studios with feedback on everything from the length of a camera shot to what color dress a character should wear. "Our goal is how we can drive audiences from YouTube, from TikTok, from Instagram to our platform, and also create those kinds of synergies [with] legacy media," he said. Holywater recently adapted Season 3 of Fox's reality TV hit "Farmer Wants a Wife" into a microseries fit for the platform. The company also plans to create a scripted series featuring 30 three-minute episodes inspired by Fox's "Fear Factor: House of Fear." Holywater currently relies on a combination of subscription fees, which make up about 80% of its revenue, and money from advertisers. Nesvit said the company is also exploring incorporating brand integrations. The company is already profitable, its co-founders said. Co-founder Anatolii Kasianov said creating the videos is "very cost efficient," with an estimated expense of between $150,000 and $200,000 for an average 70-minute series. The company's partnerships with content studios, he said, help to bring down customer acquisition costs. "You attract organically the audience that loves that [intellectual property]," he said. Hollywood moves in While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house. Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun, who have collectively held leadership roles at NBCUniversal, Showtime, Warner Bros. Discovery and ABC, have jointly founded a microdrama startup called aTwist. The company, which officially launched in September, has garnered tens of millions of views as of late November across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, where content lives in addition to the app. "One of the specialties that we have is really what it means to be a great storyteller," Rovner told CNBC in an interview. During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest." "A lot of our competitors' completion rates are very low, their churn rates are very high," Rovner said. "They can often bring people into the store but they can't keep them." The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data. The market intelligence firm notes that the number of users lost in each quarter this year has roughly equaled the number of users gained.

But that arc has changed, according to Hernan Lopez, the head of Owl, who was previously president and CEO of Fox International.“Today, you hear anecdotally of many people coming to L.A. and getting their first job through a vertical drama.”

extraction.body: Intel has beaten its own guidance for seven straight quarters, with second-quarter revenue up 25%. Demand for its CPUs continues to outrun supply as AI moves into inference and agentic workloads. Intel Foundry losses are narrowing, with management targeting breakeven by late 2027 or 2028. Shares of Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) are up about 180% over the past year, as of Oct. 12, reflecting growing demand for its chips for artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. The stock is more expensive than it was a year ago, but the prospect of sustainable revenue growth from AI leaves room for further gains over the next several years. "AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, and as we continue to execute, Intel is well-positioned to capture sustainable growth across our CPU franchise, ASICs, advanced packaging, and vast wafer foundry network," CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated in the 2026 second-quarter earnings report. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Here are three reasons the stock is a buy heading into 2027. Intel has topped its own financial expectations for seven straight quarters. Beating guidance repeatedly shows the company is executing well against its goals and managing its factories and costs, which can support a higher stock price over time as investors gain confidence. Here are the key highlights from the Q2 earnings report that point to building momentum in the business: Revenue rose 25% year over year to $16.1 billion -- the company's strongest growth in more than 15 years. Non-GAAP gross margin (the share of revenue left after production costs) reached 41.8%, more than 12 points higher than a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.42 more than doubled the guidance of $0.20, and reversed a loss of $0.10 in the year-ago quarter. Higher revenue, better manufacturing yields (more working chips per wafer), and stronger average selling prices drove the strong results, with data-center and AI sales growing 59% to $6.3 billion. AI-related businesses made up roughly 70% of Intel's total revenue in the quarter. CFO David Zinsner said the near-term goal was to get gross margins "comfortably into the 40s" every quarter -- implying the potential for more gains over its Q2 gross margin. Overall, the prospect of expanding margins is a positive for the stock heading into 2027. AI will need a massive number of central processing units (CPUs), as well as specialized accelerators and graphics processing units (GPUs) . CPUs have proven more effective at handling orchestration, data movement, and storage around AI training and inference. The growing use of AI agents (software that performs tasks autonomously) will put more strain on existing compute capacity and is a long-term tailwind for Intel. Intel faces growing competition in the CPU market from Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia . But all these companies should continue to post robust growth, since demand for CPUs continues to outrun supply. AI agents require a four to six times increase in CPU requirements, which is leading to higher core counts and more stable pricing. Beyond servers, Intel sees further opportunities in edge computing and physical AI systems such as industrial equipment and robotics. These opportunities support analysts' expectations that Intel's revenue will increase by 21% in 2027, reaching $78 billion. Intel's foundry efforts (making chips for other companies) and advanced packaging technology, which connects multiple chips into more powerful processing systems, are showing progress. The 18A process is in high-volume production. Better yields and execution in ramping new technologies mean Intel can produce more chips at lower cost, which improves margins and can attract outside customers for Intel's foundry. Management sees its advanced packaging business potentially reaching billions of dollars in revenue with attractive margins. Revenue is expected to ramp more meaningfully in the second half of 2027 and can also open the door to larger foundry deals. Intel's foundry posted a Q2 operating loss of $2.1 billion, although the loss narrowed by $348 million over Q1. The foundry's persistent losses have been an overhang on the stock in recent years, but management is working to bring this business to breakeven by the end of 2027 or into 2028. Narrowing losses at Intel Foundry could support a higher stock price in 2027. Intel's shares are not cheap, trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 67 on 2026 earnings estimates. Even so, accelerating growth, expanding margins, and long-term opportunities in physical AI could still support excellent returns for investors in 2027 and beyond. The forward multiple drops to 49 on 2027 estimates, with analysts expecting 69% annualized earnings growth in the next several years. passages: The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs.

AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC.

Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power.
That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007.

Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features.

Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations.
This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China.

AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC.

Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power.
That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007.

Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features.

Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations.
This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China.

extraction.body: In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.The Financial Times lays out how Nvidia came to dominate the AI chip market.Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud computing company she ran, is still under investigation by the US justice department for allegedly circumventing export bans by obtaining computer chips for use by China.Nvidia had almost $20 billion in sales to China last year.

The company can sell graphics cards for personal computers and server chips with lower processing power to China without a special license.

passages: Oracle says student teams in Kenya built climate and sustainability tools on its cloud and low-code stack at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon, and the company’s own write-up carries the headline “Students drive sustainable innovation with Oracle Technology at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya.” According to Oracle’s blog, the event drew 267 applications, narrowed them to 12 finalist teams, and ended with an in-person pitching day at Strathmore University on 16 October 2026.
Twelve teams reached the finals, a figure that both Oracle and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report confirm.
Using only those two numbers, the finalist group is a small fraction of the applicant pool.
We will not turn that into a precise acceptance rate, because the reports do not say whether the 267 figure counts individual students or teams.
A rate built on an unclear denominator would mislead.
The conflicts affect only the precise calendar, and readers planning to follow the event next year should check the organizers’ own pages for the final schedule.
TVET refers to technical and vocational education and training, so the hackathon was not limited to degree-track computer science students.
An event listing for the hackathon adds the administrative detail.
It gives a team size of two to five members, a submission deadline of 30 September 2026, finalist notification on 6 October 2026 and a virtual bootcamp from 12 to 15 October 2026.
We treat that listing as a planning document rather than a results report, since it was written before the event ran.
One date inside it conflicts with the rest of the record, and we cover that below.
None of the available reports quote a named speaker, a judge or a student.
Where this article reaches past the reported facts, it says so and labels the passage as analysis.
Hackathons have worked as recruiting and training tools for well over a decade, and technology firms treat them as a low-cost way to meet students.
Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica strengthens its position as a convening point for student innovation, and Oracle Kenya gets a visible presence on campus.

For readers who track how developers pick up tools, from AI editors (see our Antigravity vs Cursor price comparison ) to low-code platforms, a student hackathon is a useful window into what the next cohort of engineers will reach for first.
Splitting the event this way lets a hackathon reach students who live far from Nairobi, since the learning and building phase needs only a laptop and a connection.
A team that arrives with an idea but no cloud experience has to learn a platform, wire up data and produce a demo inside that window.
The takeaway: the verified record shows a well-subscribed student event, a clear Oracle technology stack, a sustainability brief and a winner with a practical farming tool.

extraction.body: Oracle says student teams in Kenya built climate and sustainability tools on its cloud and low-code stack at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon, and the company’s own write-up carries the headline “Students drive sustainable innovation with Oracle Technology at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya.” According to Oracle’s blog, the event drew 267 applications, narrowed them to 12 finalist teams, and ended with an in-person pitching day at Strathmore University on 16 October 2026. Team Daraja took the title. A separate report from @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University, which names Oracle Kenya as a partner, fills in what the winners actually built. It describes Team Daraja’s entry as an AI-powered early-warning tool meant to help farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts and floods. That is a concrete, practical product idea, and it is the kind of project a developer audience can judge on its merits. This story sits on the coding-tools desk because of what the students used and learned. Oracle names Oracle Academy, Oracle APEX and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure as the technology behind the event, and it lists application development, cloud technologies, artificial intelligence and problem-solving as the skills on offer. For readers who track how developers pick up tools, from AI editors (see our Antigravity vs Cursor price comparison ) to low-code platforms, a student hackathon is a useful window into what the next cohort of engineers will reach for first. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The core facts come from two kinds of source. Oracle’s blog post is the main account, and it frames the event as a program for university and TVET students across Kenya. TVET refers to technical and vocational education and training, so the hackathon was not limited to degree-track computer science students. That matters for the story, because it widens the pool of people who got hands-on time with cloud and application-development tools. Oracle describes the format as four days of virtual learning, technical mentoring and solution development, followed by the in-person pitching event at Strathmore University. The company identifies Team Daraja as the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon Champions. The @iLabAfrica report, which names @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University and Oracle Kenya, confirms the 12 finalist teams and supplies the description of the winning solution. An event listing for the hackathon adds the administrative detail. It gives a team size of two to five members, a submission deadline of 30 September 2026, finalist notification on 6 October 2026 and a virtual bootcamp from 12 to 15 October 2026. We treat that listing as a planning document rather than a results report, since it was written before the event ran. One date inside it conflicts with the rest of the record, and we cover that below. None of the available reports quote a named speaker, a judge or a student. The reports also give no prize amounts, no judging rubric and no list of the 12 finalist teams beyond the winner. We will not fill those gaps with guesses. Where this article reaches past the reported facts, it says so and labels the passage as analysis. Oracle reports 267 applications for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. Twelve teams reached the finals, a figure that both Oracle and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report confirm. Using only those two numbers, the finalist group is a small fraction of the applicant pool. We will not turn that into a precise acceptance rate, because the reports do not say whether the 267 figure counts individual students or teams. A rate built on an unclear denominator would mislead. The table below gathers every figure the fact record supports, with the source for each. Treat the right-hand column as the guide to how much weight each number deserves. The team-size rule is worth a second look. A cap of five and a floor of two pushes students to split work the way a small product team would, with one person on the data model, another on the interface and another on the pitch. That structure rewards collaboration over solo heroics, and it mirrors how real engineering squads operate. Oracle describes a two-stage design. Students first spent four days online, learning tools, getting technical mentoring and building solutions. The finalists then met in person at Strathmore University to pitch on 16 October 2026. Splitting the event this way lets a hackathon reach students who live far from Nairobi, since the learning and building phase needs only a laptop and a connection. The event listing places the virtual bootcamp on 12 to 15 October 2026, which matches Oracle’s four-day count. Four days is short. A team that arrives with an idea but no cloud experience has to learn a platform, wire up data and produce a demo inside that window. Mentoring is what makes this workable, and Oracle lists technical mentoring as a named part of the program. Low-code tooling helps here. A platform that generates forms, reports and data screens from a database schema lets a student team spend its limited hours on the problem logic instead of boilerplate. Oracle names APEX as part of the toolkit, and we return to why that choice shapes the projects later in this piece. The win also fits a pattern in applied-AI education. Student projects that tie a model to a real local hazard tend to stand out against generic demos, because judges can picture an actual user. We cannot confirm what the judges prioritized in Nairobi, since no judging criteria appear in the reports. We can say the winning idea matched the sustainability theme directly. Oracle names six challenge areas for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. They are climate-smart agriculture, waste and the circular economy, carbon reduction, sustainable transport, climate data and water stewardship. The list covers both physical-world problems, such as waste and transport, and data-centric ones, such as climate data. That mix gave teams room to pick a problem that matched their skills. The reports do not say which tracks drew the most entries, so we cannot rank them by popularity. What we can observe is that nearly every track depends on data collection and reporting, which is exactly what a low-code, database-backed platform handles well. A team building a waste-tracking app or a water-usage dashboard can reach a working demo quickly with that kind of tooling. Oracle names three technology pillars for the event. Oracle Academy is the company’s education program. Oracle APEX is its low-code application platform. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is the cloud where applications run. The table below separates what Oracle reports from general background on each product, so readers can see where the reported record ends. The last row matters. Oracle lists artificial intelligence as a skill area but does not name the AI services students used, so we do not know whether Team Daraja’s model ran on Oracle’s own AI offerings or on other tools. Readers should not assume the winning system was built entirely inside the Oracle stack. The record on this story contains two discrepancies, and honest coverage has to name them. First, the event listing gives the in-person pitching date as 16 October 2025, which clashes with the event’s 2026 title and with the reports that state 16 October 2026. We treat the 2025 date as unconfirmed for the 2026 event and use 16 October 2026, the date Oracle and the Strathmore report support. Second, one official report describes a two-day online hackathon on 14 to 15 October 2026, while Oracle’s account describes four days of virtual work and a program ending on 16 October 2026. Both could be partly right if the online stage had different phases, or one report could simply be describing a different part of the program. The available material does not settle it. The table lays out the conflicts side by side. None of this changes the headline facts. The 267 applications, the 12 finalists, the Strathmore venue and Team Daraja’s title all hold up across the sources we have. The conflicts affect only the precise calendar, and readers planning to follow the event next year should check the organizers’ own pages for the final schedule. Hackathons have worked as recruiting and training tools for well over a decade, and technology firms treat them as a low-cost way to meet students. In Kenya, university innovation hubs such as Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica have long hosted this kind of event, and they give companies a ready venue, a pool of students and a mentoring network. Oracle’s choice to partner with a university hub rather than run the event alone follows that established playbook. Climate-themed hackathons have grown more common as sustainability moved up the corporate agenda. Pairing a green theme with cloud and AI tools lets a vendor show its platform solving problems that governments and donors care about. For students, the theme adds meaning to what could otherwise be a generic coding exercise. We lack figures on how many such events ran in Kenya this year, so we will not size the trend. Developer culture around tools also shifts fast, and what students learn today may not match what their employers use. Survey data on editor choice shows how slowly some habits change. Our look at Vim, Neovim and Helix usage shares shows long-lived tools holding ground while newer entrants fight for a small slice. Platform vendors know this, which is why they court learners early. The hackathon’s edge is the combination of deadline pressure, a live audience and expert help in one place. Its limit is lock-in, since students leave knowing one vendor’s tools best. A smart organizer balances this by teaching general skills, such as data modeling and cloud basics, that transfer. Oracle lists problem-solving and application development among the targeted skills, which suggests at least some of the learning is portable. Team Daraja took the title.

A separate report from @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University, which names Oracle Kenya as a partner, fills in what the winners actually built. It describes Team Daraja’s entry as an AI-powered early-warning tool meant to help farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts and floods. The core facts come from two kinds of source. Oracle’s blog post is the main account, and it frames the event as a program for university and TVET students across Kenya. TVET refers to technical and vocational education and training, so the hackathon was not limited to degree-track computer science students. That matters for the story, because it widens the pool of people who got hands-on time with cloud and application-development tools.

Oracle describes the format as four days of virtual learning, technical mentoring and solution development, followed by the in-person pitching event at Strathmore University. The company identifies Team Daraja as the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon Champions. The @iLabAfrica report, which names @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University and Oracle Kenya, confirms the 12 finalist teams and supplies the description of the winning solution.

An event listing for the hackathon adds the administrative detail. It gives a team size of two to five members, a submission deadline of 30 September 2026, finalist notification on 6 October 2026 and a virtual bootcamp from 12 to 15 October 2026. We treat that listing as a planning document rather than a results report, since it was written before the event ran. One date inside it conflicts with the rest of the record, and we cover that below.

None of the available reports quote a named speaker, a judge or a student. The reports also give no prize amounts, no judging rubric and no list of the 12 finalist teams beyond the winner. We will not fill those gaps with guesses. Where this article reaches past the reported facts, it says so and labels the passage as analysis.

Using only those two numbers, the finalist group is a small fraction of the applicant pool. The table below gathers every figure the fact record supports, with the source for each. Treat the right-hand column as the guide to how much weight each number deserves.

The team-size rule is worth a second look. A cap of five and a floor of two pushes students to split work the way a small product team would, with one person on the data model, another on the interface and another on the pitch. That structure rewards collaboration over solo heroics, and it mirrors how real engineering squads operate.

Oracle describes a two-stage design. Students first spent four days online, learning tools, getting technical mentoring and building solutions. The finalists then met in person at Strathmore University to pitch on 16 October 2026. Splitting the event this way lets a hackathon reach students who live far from Nairobi, since the learning and building phase needs only a laptop and a connection.

The event listing places the virtual bootcamp on 12 to 15 October 2026, which matches Oracle’s four-day count. Four days is short. A team that arrives with an idea but no cloud experience has to learn a platform, wire up data and produce a demo inside that window. Mentoring is what makes this workable, and Oracle lists technical mentoring as a named part of the program.

Low-code tooling helps here. A platform that generates forms, reports and data screens from a database schema lets a student team spend its limited hours on the problem logic instead of boilerplate. Oracle names APEX as part of the toolkit, and we return to why that choice shapes the projects later in this piece.

The win also fits a pattern in applied-AI education. Student projects that tie a model to a real local hazard tend to stand out against generic demos, because judges can picture an actual user. We cannot confirm what the judges prioritized in Nairobi, since no judging criteria appear in the reports. We can say the winning idea matched the sustainability theme directly.

The reports do not say which tracks drew the most entries, so we cannot rank them by popularity. What we can observe is that nearly every track depends on data collection and reporting, which is exactly what a low-code, database-backed platform handles well. A team building a waste-tracking app or a water-usage dashboard can reach a working demo quickly with that kind of tooling.

sources.title: Students drive sustainable innovation with Oracle Technology at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya - Oracle Blogs
passages: Across Kenya, students already are using technology to respond to environmental challenges in their communities.
At the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon, Oracle and Strathmore University created a platform for those ideas to take shape.
Their AI-powered early-warning solution helps farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts, and floods, strengthening agricultural resilience and supporting timely decision-making.
Daraja’s innovation demonstrates how practical technology can help communities prepare for climate-related challenges and protect livelihoods.
Oracle Academy thanks the Master of Ceremony Eng.
Together with Strathmore University and iLabAfrica , we are helping young innovators turn ideas into solutions that can create lasting impact.
“What stood out most during the Strathmore Oracle GreenTech Hackathon 2026 was the creativity, passion, and technical potential demonstrated by the participating teams.
It was encouraging to see young innovators leveraging Oracle technologies to tackle real-world environmental and sustainability challenges.

Beyond the technology itself, we were particularly keen on how well teams understood the problems they were solving and the practical impact their solutions could deliver,” said Billy Otieno, Enterprise AI and Cloud Solutions Architect, Oracle, and Chief Judge, GreenTech Hackathon.
The winning teams will continue to receive support through three months of business coaching, helping them explore how to develop their solutions further.
“Sustainable innovation must balance profit, people, and planet.

The hackathon gives students an opportunity to test those possibilities with support from Oracle Academy,” noted David Bunei, Oracle Kenya Country Director & Senior Director, Public Sector, Sub-Saharan Africa.
Oracle Academy helps institutions build hands-on computing skills by providing access to Oracle technology for teaching, student learning, and academic research.
The hackathon received 267 applications, and 12 finalist teams progressed to the Grand Finale to present their solutions before an Oracle judging panel.
Find out more about the first runners-up, second runners-up, and judges’ award winning teams in The Tech Innovations Changing How Kenya Tackles Climate Challenges .

extraction.body: Oracle says student teams in Kenya built climate and sustainability tools on its cloud and low-code stack at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon, and the company’s own write-up carries the headline “Students drive sustainable innovation with Oracle Technology at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya.” According to Oracle’s blog, the event drew 267 applications, narrowed them to 12 finalist teams, and ended with an in-person pitching day at Strathmore University on 16 October 2026. Team Daraja took the title. A separate report from @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University, which names Oracle Kenya as a partner, fills in what the winners actually built. It describes Team Daraja’s entry as an AI-powered early-warning tool meant to help farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts and floods. That is a concrete, practical product idea, and it is the kind of project a developer audience can judge on its merits. This story sits on the coding-tools desk because of what the students used and learned. Oracle names Oracle Academy, Oracle APEX and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure as the technology behind the event, and it lists application development, cloud technologies, artificial intelligence and problem-solving as the skills on offer. For readers who track how developers pick up tools, from AI editors (see our Antigravity vs Cursor price comparison ) to low-code platforms, a student hackathon is a useful window into what the next cohort of engineers will reach for first. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The core facts come from two kinds of source. Oracle’s blog post is the main account, and it frames the event as a program for university and TVET students across Kenya. TVET refers to technical and vocational education and training, so the hackathon was not limited to degree-track computer science students. That matters for the story, because it widens the pool of people who got hands-on time with cloud and application-development tools. Oracle describes the format as four days of virtual learning, technical mentoring and solution development, followed by the in-person pitching event at Strathmore University. The company identifies Team Daraja as the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon Champions. The @iLabAfrica report, which names @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University and Oracle Kenya, confirms the 12 finalist teams and supplies the description of the winning solution. An event listing for the hackathon adds the administrative detail. It gives a team size of two to five members, a submission deadline of 30 September 2026, finalist notification on 6 October 2026 and a virtual bootcamp from 12 to 15 October 2026. We treat that listing as a planning document rather than a results report, since it was written before the event ran. One date inside it conflicts with the rest of the record, and we cover that below. None of the available reports quote a named speaker, a judge or a student. The reports also give no prize amounts, no judging rubric and no list of the 12 finalist teams beyond the winner. We will not fill those gaps with guesses. Where this article reaches past the reported facts, it says so and labels the passage as analysis. Oracle reports 267 applications for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. Twelve teams reached the finals, a figure that both Oracle and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report confirm. Using only those two numbers, the finalist group is a small fraction of the applicant pool. We will not turn that into a precise acceptance rate, because the reports do not say whether the 267 figure counts individual students or teams. A rate built on an unclear denominator would mislead. The table below gathers every figure the fact record supports, with the source for each. Treat the right-hand column as the guide to how much weight each number deserves. The team-size rule is worth a second look. A cap of five and a floor of two pushes students to split work the way a small product team would, with one person on the data model, another on the interface and another on the pitch. That structure rewards collaboration over solo heroics, and it mirrors how real engineering squads operate. Oracle describes a two-stage design. Students first spent four days online, learning tools, getting technical mentoring and building solutions. The finalists then met in person at Strathmore University to pitch on 16 October 2026. Splitting the event this way lets a hackathon reach students who live far from Nairobi, since the learning and building phase needs only a laptop and a connection. The event listing places the virtual bootcamp on 12 to 15 October 2026, which matches Oracle’s four-day count. Four days is short. A team that arrives with an idea but no cloud experience has to learn a platform, wire up data and produce a demo inside that window. Mentoring is what makes this workable, and Oracle lists technical mentoring as a named part of the program. Low-code tooling helps here. A platform that generates forms, reports and data screens from a database schema lets a student team spend its limited hours on the problem logic instead of boilerplate. Oracle names APEX as part of the toolkit, and we return to why that choice shapes the projects later in this piece. The win also fits a pattern in applied-AI education. Student projects that tie a model to a real local hazard tend to stand out against generic demos, because judges can picture an actual user. We cannot confirm what the judges prioritized in Nairobi, since no judging criteria appear in the reports. We can say the winning idea matched the sustainability theme directly. Oracle names six challenge areas for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. They are climate-smart agriculture, waste and the circular economy, carbon reduction, sustainable transport, climate data and water stewardship. The list covers both physical-world problems, such as waste and transport, and data-centric ones, such as climate data. That mix gave teams room to pick a problem that matched their skills. The reports do not say which tracks drew the most entries, so we cannot rank them by popularity. What we can observe is that nearly every track depends on data collection and reporting, which is exactly what a low-code, database-backed platform handles well. A team building a waste-tracking app or a water-usage dashboard can reach a working demo quickly with that kind of tooling. Oracle names three technology pillars for the event. Oracle Academy is the company’s education program. Oracle APEX is its low-code application platform. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is the cloud where applications run. The table below separates what Oracle reports from general background on each product, so readers can see where the reported record ends. The last row matters. Oracle lists artificial intelligence as a skill area but does not name the AI services students used, so we do not know whether Team Daraja’s model ran on Oracle’s own AI offerings or on other tools. Readers should not assume the winning system was built entirely inside the Oracle stack. The record on this story contains two discrepancies, and honest coverage has to name them. First, the event listing gives the in-person pitching date as 16 October 2025, which clashes with the event’s 2026 title and with the reports that state 16 October 2026. We treat the 2025 date as unconfirmed for the 2026 event and use 16 October 2026, the date Oracle and the Strathmore report support. Second, one official report describes a two-day online hackathon on 14 to 15 October 2026, while Oracle’s account describes four days of virtual work and a program ending on 16 October 2026. Both could be partly right if the online stage had different phases, or one report could simply be describing a different part of the program. The available material does not settle it. The table lays out the conflicts side by side. None of this changes the headline facts. The 267 applications, the 12 finalists, the Strathmore venue and Team Daraja’s title all hold up across the sources we have. The conflicts affect only the precise calendar, and readers planning to follow the event next year should check the organizers’ own pages for the final schedule. Hackathons have worked as recruiting and training tools for well over a decade, and technology firms treat them as a low-cost way to meet students. In Kenya, university innovation hubs such as Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica have long hosted this kind of event, and they give companies a ready venue, a pool of students and a mentoring network. Oracle’s choice to partner with a university hub rather than run the event alone follows that established playbook. Climate-themed hackathons have grown more common as sustainability moved up the corporate agenda. Pairing a green theme with cloud and AI tools lets a vendor show its platform solving problems that governments and donors care about. For students, the theme adds meaning to what could otherwise be a generic coding exercise. We lack figures on how many such events ran in Kenya this year, so we will not size the trend. Developer culture around tools also shifts fast, and what students learn today may not match what their employers use. Survey data on editor choice shows how slowly some habits change. Our look at Vim, Neovim and Helix usage shares shows long-lived tools holding ground while newer entrants fight for a small slice. Platform vendors know this, which is why they court learners early. The hackathon’s edge is the combination of deadline pressure, a live audience and expert help in one place. Its limit is lock-in, since students leave knowing one vendor’s tools best. A smart organizer balances this by teaching general skills, such as data modeling and cloud basics, that transfer. Oracle lists problem-solving and application development among the targeted skills, which suggests at least some of the learning is portable. One event will not shift a labor market, and the reports give no hiring or funding outcomes. What 267 applications do show is demand. Hundreds of students wanted four days of cloud and AI training on a sustainability brief, and that is a useful signal for employers, universities and the vendors competing for developer attention. The TVET angle deserves attention. Open calls that include technical and vocational students bring a different group into the pipeline than events limited to university computer science departments. Employers who need applied builders, rather than researchers, may find that group valuable. This is our reading, and the reports do not break down the applicants by institution type. For Oracle, the commercial upside is indirect. The company gains goodwill, a base of students who know Oracle Academy, APEX and its cloud, and a story that links its products to climate goals. We have no figures on cost, sponsorship size or conversion to paid usage, so we cannot size the return. The reports contain no prices or product specifications. Beyond that, local partners gain too. Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica strengthens its position as a convening point for student innovation, and Oracle Kenya gets a visible presence on campus. Winning teams such as Team Daraja may find doors open to mentors, pilots and funders, although no such follow-up has been announced. These are our forecasts, offered as analysis and not as reported facts. Each rests on the pattern of the reported event. The takeaway: the verified record shows a well-subscribed student event, a clear Oracle technology stack, a sustainability brief and a winner with a practical farming tool. The gaps are real, but the core story holds across Oracle’s blog and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report. Oracle’s blog identifies Team Daraja as the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon Champions. The Strathmore @iLabAfrica report describes their entry as an AI-powered early-warning solution to help farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts and floods. Oracle and Strathmore University ran the event. A separate Strathmore report names @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University and Oracle Kenya as the partners. Oracle reports 267 applications and 12 finalist teams. The reports do not say whether the 267 figure counts individuals or teams. Oracle and the Strathmore report give 16 October 2026 at Strathmore University. An event listing shows 16 October 2025, which we treat as unconfirmed for the 2026 event.

For readers who track how developers pick up tools, from AI editors (see our Antigravity vs Cursor price comparison ) to low-code platforms, a student hackathon is a useful window into what the next cohort of engineers will reach for first.
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

The core facts come from two kinds of source. Oracle’s blog post is the main account, and it frames the event as a program for university and TVET students across Kenya. TVET refers to technical and vocational education and training, so the hackathon was not limited to degree-track computer science students. That matters for the story, because it widens the pool of people who got hands-on time with cloud and application-development tools.

Oracle describes the format as four days of virtual learning, technical mentoring and solution development, followed by the in-person pitching event at Strathmore University. The company identifies Team Daraja as the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon Champions. The @iLabAfrica report, which names @iLabAfrica at Strathmore University and Oracle Kenya, confirms the 12 finalist teams and supplies the description of the winning solution.

An event listing for the hackathon adds the administrative detail. It gives a team size of two to five members, a submission deadline of 30 September 2026, finalist notification on 6 October 2026 and a virtual bootcamp from 12 to 15 October 2026. We treat that listing as a planning document rather than a results report, since it was written before the event ran. One date inside it conflicts with the rest of the record, and we cover that below.

None of the available reports quote a named speaker, a judge or a student. The reports also give no prize amounts, no judging rubric and no list of the 12 finalist teams beyond the winner. We will not fill those gaps with guesses. Where this article reaches past the reported facts, it says so and labels the passage as analysis.

Oracle reports 267 applications for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. Twelve teams reached the finals, a figure that both Oracle and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report confirm. Using only those two numbers, the finalist group is a small fraction of the applicant pool. We will not turn that into a precise acceptance rate, because the reports do not say whether the 267 figure counts individual students or teams. A rate built on an unclear denominator would mislead.
The table below gathers every figure the fact record supports, with the source for each. Treat the right-hand column as the guide to how much weight each number deserves.

The team-size rule is worth a second look. A cap of five and a floor of two pushes students to split work the way a small product team would, with one person on the data model, another on the interface and another on the pitch. That structure rewards collaboration over solo heroics, and it mirrors how real engineering squads operate.

Oracle describes a two-stage design. Students first spent four days online, learning tools, getting technical mentoring and building solutions. The finalists then met in person at Strathmore University to pitch on 16 October 2026. Splitting the event this way lets a hackathon reach students who live far from Nairobi, since the learning and building phase needs only a laptop and a connection.

The event listing places the virtual bootcamp on 12 to 15 October 2026, which matches Oracle’s four-day count. Four days is short. A team that arrives with an idea but no cloud experience has to learn a platform, wire up data and produce a demo inside that window. Mentoring is what makes this workable, and Oracle lists technical mentoring as a named part of the program.

Low-code tooling helps here. A platform that generates forms, reports and data screens from a database schema lets a student team spend its limited hours on the problem logic instead of boilerplate. Oracle names APEX as part of the toolkit, and we return to why that choice shapes the projects later in this piece.

The win also fits a pattern in applied-AI education. Student projects that tie a model to a real local hazard tend to stand out against generic demos, because judges can picture an actual user. We cannot confirm what the judges prioritized in Nairobi, since no judging criteria appear in the reports. We can say the winning idea matched the sustainability theme directly.

Oracle names six challenge areas for the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon. They are climate-smart agriculture, waste and the circular economy, carbon reduction, sustainable transport, climate data and water stewardship. The list covers both physical-world problems, such as waste and transport, and data-centric ones, such as climate data. That mix gave teams room to pick a problem that matched their skills.

The reports do not say which tracks drew the most entries, so we cannot rank them by popularity. What we can observe is that nearly every track depends on data collection and reporting, which is exactly what a low-code, database-backed platform handles well. A team building a waste-tracking app or a water-usage dashboard can reach a working demo quickly with that kind of tooling.

Oracle names three technology pillars for the event. Oracle Academy is the company’s education program. Oracle APEX is its low-code application platform. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is the cloud where applications run. The table below separates what Oracle reports from general background on each product, so readers can see where the reported record ends.

The last row matters. Oracle lists artificial intelligence as a skill area but does not name the AI services students used, so we do not know whether Team Daraja’s model ran on Oracle’s own AI offerings or on other tools. Readers should not assume the winning system was built entirely inside the Oracle stack.

The record on this story contains two discrepancies, and honest coverage has to name them. First, the event listing gives the in-person pitching date as 16 October 2025, which clashes with the event’s 2026 title and with the reports that state 16 October 2026. We treat the 2025 date as unconfirmed for the 2026 event and use 16 October 2026, the date Oracle and the Strathmore report support.

Second, one official report describes a two-day online hackathon on 14 to 15 October 2026, while Oracle’s account describes four days of virtual work and a program ending on 16 October 2026. Both could be partly right if the online stage had different phases, or one report could simply be describing a different part of the program. The available material does not settle it. The table lays out the conflicts side by side.

None of this changes the headline facts. The 267 applications, the 12 finalists, the Strathmore venue and Team Daraja’s title all hold up across the sources we have. The conflicts affect only the precise calendar, and readers planning to follow the event next year should check the organizers’ own pages for the final schedule.

Hackathons have worked as recruiting and training tools for well over a decade, and technology firms treat them as a low-cost way to meet students. In Kenya, university innovation hubs such as Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica have long hosted this kind of event, and they give companies a ready venue, a pool of students and a mentoring network. Oracle’s choice to partner with a university hub rather than run the event alone follows that established playbook.

Climate-themed hackathons have grown more common as sustainability moved up the corporate agenda. Pairing a green theme with cloud and AI tools lets a vendor show its platform solving problems that governments and donors care about. For students, the theme adds meaning to what could otherwise be a generic coding exercise. We lack figures on how many such events ran in Kenya this year, so we will not size the trend.

Developer culture around tools also shifts fast, and what students learn today may not match what their employers use. Survey data on editor choice shows how slowly some habits change. Our look at Vim, Neovim and Helix usage shares shows long-lived tools holding ground while newer entrants fight for a small slice. Platform vendors know this, which is why they court learners early.

The hackathon’s edge is the combination of deadline pressure, a live audience and expert help in one place. Its limit is lock-in, since students leave knowing one vendor’s tools best. A smart organizer balances this by teaching general skills, such as data modeling and cloud basics, that transfer. Oracle lists problem-solving and application development among the targeted skills, which suggests at least some of the learning is portable.

One event will not shift a labor market, and the reports give no hiring or funding outcomes. What 267 applications do show is demand. Hundreds of students wanted four days of cloud and AI training on a sustainability brief, and that is a useful signal for employers, universities and the vendors competing for developer attention.

The TVET angle deserves attention. Open calls that include technical and vocational students bring a different group into the pipeline than events limited to university computer science departments. Employers who need applied builders, rather than researchers, may find that group valuable. This is our reading, and the reports do not break down the applicants by institution type.

For Oracle, the commercial upside is indirect. The company gains goodwill, a base of students who know Oracle Academy, APEX and its cloud, and a story that links its products to climate goals. We have no figures on cost, sponsorship size or conversion to paid usage, so we cannot size the return. The reports contain no prices or product specifications.

Beyond that, local partners gain too. Strathmore’s @iLabAfrica strengthens its position as a convening point for student innovation, and Oracle Kenya gets a visible presence on campus. Winning teams such as Team Daraja may find doors open to mentors, pilots and funders, although no such follow-up has been announced.
These are our forecasts, offered as analysis and not as reported facts. Each rests on the pattern of the reported event.

The takeaway: the verified record shows a well-subscribed student event, a clear Oracle technology stack, a sustainability brief and a winner with a practical farming tool. The gaps are real, but the core story holds across Oracle’s blog and the Strathmore @iLabAfrica report.

sources.title: Students drive sustainable innovation with Oracle Technology at the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon in Kenya - Oracle Blogs
passages: Across Kenya, students already are using technology to respond to environmental challenges in their communities.
At the 2026 Green Tech Hackathon, Oracle and Strathmore University created a platform for those ideas to take shape.
Their AI-powered early-warning solution helps farmers anticipate livestock diseases, droughts, and floods, strengthening agricultural resilience and supporting timely decision-making.
Daraja’s innovation demonstrates how practical technology can help communities prepare for climate-related challenges and protect livelihoods.
Oracle Academy thanks the Master of Ceremony Eng.
Together with Strathmore University and iLabAfrica , we are helping young innovators turn ideas into solutions that can create lasting impact.
“What stood out most during the Strathmore Oracle GreenTech Hackathon 2026 was the creativity, passion, and technical potential demonstrated by the participating teams.
It was encouraging to see young innovators leveraging Oracle technologies to tackle real-world environmental and sustainability challenges.

Beyond the technology itself, we were particularly keen on how well teams understood the problems they were solving and the practical impact their solutions could deliver,” said Billy Otieno, Enterprise AI and Cloud Solutions Architect, Oracle, and Chief Judge, GreenTech Hackathon.
The winning teams will continue to receive support through three months of business coaching, helping them explore how to develop their solutions further.
“Sustainable innovation must balance profit, people, and planet.

The hackathon gives students an opportunity to test those possibilities with support from Oracle Academy,” noted David Bunei, Oracle Kenya Country Director & Senior Director, Public Sector, Sub-Saharan Africa.
Oracle Academy helps institutions build hands-on computing skills by providing access to Oracle technology for teaching, student learning, and academic research.
The hackathon received 267 applications, and 12 finalist teams progressed to the Grand Finale to present their solutions before an Oracle judging panel.
Find out more about the first runners-up, second runners-up, and judges’ award winning teams in The Tech Innovations Changing How Kenya Tackles Climate Challenges .

Historically, the answer has been mixed. Investors who held Bitcoin for ten years saw considerable profits. However, those who bought in five years ago have seen only an 11.4% increase, while larger investors are still cashing out.
So is Bitcoin a good investment for building wealth after a 50% drop?

Even Bitcoin enthusiasts are tempering their expectations for future growth. Anthony Pompliano, a well-known Bitcoin advocate, said on his podcast in August that he expects Bitcoin's future returns to be much lower than in the past. He doesn't foresee annual returns of 60% to 70% like those seen previously over the next decade.

This outlook creates a challenging environment for Bitcoin, especially when compared to stocks. For instance, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY )—which tracks the 500 largest U.S. companies—has returned 223.5% over the last decade and 56.2% over the past five years. Anyone investing in Bitcoin must aim to outperform these returns, or they might find that a standard index fund offers a more stable investment.

Bitcoin has faced steep drops before. It fell 68% from $1,127 in November 2013 to $361 by April 2014, then recovered and set new all-time highs after each major decline. Our review of Bitcoin's 50% drops covers each one, and timing significantly shaped the recovery gains.

For example, an investor who purchased Bitcoin at $736 in November 2016 has seen their investment soar by about 8,150%, far exceeding the S&P 500 fund's 223.5% return over the same period. In contrast, an investor who bought at $54,487 in November 2021 has seen only an 11.4% gain after five years, falling short of the fund's 56.2% growth.
Unfortunately, those who invested this year are facing losses. Bitcoin's value has decreased by 30.6% in 2026, meaning anyone who bought on January 1 needs a 44% increase to break even.

Bitcoin is trading 19.2% below its 50-day moving average of $75,159, suggesting sellers are dominating the short-term market. Additionally, Bitcoin has tested its longer-term support levels, as shown by its 200-week average.

Given this significant downturn, many investors are questioning whether Bitcoin remains a good investment for long-term wealth-building or whether its prime days are behind it.

So is Bitcoin a good investment for building wealth after a 50% drop?

Even Bitcoin enthusiasts are tempering their expectations for future growth. Anthony Pompliano, a well-known Bitcoin advocate, said on his podcast in August that he expects Bitcoin’s future returns to be much lower than in the past. He doesn’t foresee annual returns of 60% to 70% like those seen previously over the next decade.

This outlook creates a challenging environment for Bitcoin, especially when compared to stocks. For instance, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY )—which tracks the 500 largest U.S. companies—has returned 223.5% over the last decade and 56.2% over the past five years. Anyone investing in Bitcoin must aim to outperform these returns, or they might find that a standard index fund offers a more stable investment.

This net outflow means these funds sold Bitcoin to meet redemptions, adding to selling pressure.

extraction.body: The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data . Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline. Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday. "For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month. Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals. The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration . Yet the demand for semiconductors has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday. "Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said. The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s. Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt. Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle. The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt. Got a confidential news tip?
